# Audit rules

> What the Audits view of Skribly Agent looks for - how the score works, the secret, code pattern and SEO rules, dependency checks and accessibility checks.

The **Audits** view looks at your project and at a running page. Security audits read your project, and accessibility and SEO audits read a running page. This page lists what each audit looks for. How to run an audit and send findings to an agent is on the page [Audits](/agent/audits/).

## How the score works

[Section titled “How the score works”](#how-the-score-works)

Every report starts at 100. Each finding lowers the score by its severity, and findings are sorted from most severe.

| Severity      | Points subtracted |
| ------------- | ----------------- |
| Critical      | 25                |
| High          | 10                |
| Medium        | 4                 |
| Low           | 1                 |
| Informational | 0                 |

## Secrets

[Section titled “Secrets”](#secrets)

The scan covers files tracked by git, up to 1 MB, so a project outside git is not scanned. The value is masked in the report, and lines that look like an example or placeholder are skipped.

| Rule                 | What it detects                                      | Severity |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| `aws-key`            | AWS access key                                       | Critical |
| `github-token`       | GitHub token                                         | Critical |
| `gitlab-token`       | GitLab token                                         | Critical |
| `slack-token`        | Slack token                                          | High     |
| `stripe-key`         | Live Stripe key                                      | Critical |
| `google-key`         | Google API key                                       | High     |
| `openai-key`         | OpenAI key                                           | Critical |
| `anthropic-key`      | Anthropic key                                        | Critical |
| `private-key`        | Private key                                          | Critical |
| `jwt`                | JWT in code                                          | Medium   |
| `hardcoded-password` | A password, secret, API key or token set to a string | High     |
| `env-tracked`        | A `.env` file tracked by git                         | High     |

## Risky code patterns

[Section titled “Risky code patterns”](#risky-code-patterns)

These rules skip test and fixture folders. Every finding has a file, a line and a suggested fix.

| Rule                 | What it detects                                                       | Severity |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| `eval`               | `eval(…)` in JavaScript, TypeScript, PHP or Python                    | High     |
| `new-function`       | `new Function(…)`                                                     | High     |
| `inner-html`         | HTML inserted with `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or `v-html` | Medium   |
| `shell-injection`    | Shell commands built from interpolated strings                        | High     |
| `sql-concat`         | SQL built from strings                                                | High     |
| `unsafe-deserialize` | Unsafe `pickle`, `yaml.load` or `unserialize`                         | High     |
| `tls-off`            | TLS verification turned off                                           | High     |
| `weak-hash`          | `md5` or `sha1`                                                       | Medium   |
| `cors-any`           | Requests allowed from any origin                                      | Medium   |
| `debug-on`           | Debug mode left on in configuration                                   | Medium   |
| `http-url`           | Plain `http://` address of an external system                         | Low      |

## Dependencies

[Section titled “Dependencies”](#dependencies)

The app reads exact versions from `package-lock.json`, `composer.lock`, `requirements*.txt` files that pin versions with `==`, and `poetry.lock`, then checks them against OSV.dev. Only package names and versions are sent, never code. Without a network, the audit still finishes with results from the rules.

A vulnerable package is a finding of the rule `dependency`. Its severity comes from the database entry, and its fix names the first fixed version when there is one. The audit looks up the details of the first 60 vulnerabilities.

## Accessibility

[Section titled “Accessibility”](#accessibility)

The page loads in a hidden window, and axe-core runs with the WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 tags and best-practice rules. Each rule lists up to eight elements.

Note

axe-core finds only some accessibility problems. Check keyboard use, focus order and alternative text by hand, or with the `wcag-audit` skill.

The severity of axe-core becomes the severity of the finding: critical stays critical, serious becomes high, moderate becomes medium and minor becomes low.

## SEO

[Section titled “SEO”](#seo)

| Rule                                | When it fires                                        | Severity      |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| `title`, `title-length`             | Missing title, or outside 15 to 65 characters        | High, low     |
| `description`, `description-length` | Missing description, or outside 50 to 170 characters | Medium, low   |
| `h1`, `h1-many`                     | Missing H1, or more than one                         | Medium, low   |
| `heading-order`                     | A skipped heading level                              | Low           |
| `canonical`                         | Missing canonical link                               | Low           |
| `lang`                              | Missing `lang` on `<html>`                           | Medium        |
| `viewport`                          | Missing meta viewport                                | High          |
| `noindex`                           | `noindex` in meta robots                             | High          |
| `https`                             | Page without HTTPS                                   | High          |
| `img-alt`                           | Images without `alt`                                 | Medium        |
| `link-text`                         | Links without text                                   | Low           |
| `og`                                | Missing `og:title` or `og:image`                     | Low           |
| `structured-data`                   | No JSON-LD                                           | Informational |
| `favicon`                           | Missing icon link                                    | Low           |
| `dom-size`                          | More than 1500 elements                              | Low           |
| `page-weight`                       | More than 3000 KB transferred                        | Medium        |
| `load-time`                         | Load event after more than 4 seconds                 | Medium        |
| `robots`, `robots-block`            | Missing `robots.txt`, or everything disallowed       | Low, high     |
| `sitemap`                           | No sitemap                                           | Low           |
| `broken:<url>`                      | Internal link with status 400 or higher              | Medium        |

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Audits](/agent/audits/)Run an audit, select findings and send them to an agent.

[Skills catalog](/skills/catalog/)Audit skills that run from any agent.

[Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/)What audits send, and where.

# Audits

> Run security, accessibility and SEO audits in Skribly Agent, read the score and findings, and send selected findings to an agent to fix.

The **Audits** view checks your project for security problems (secrets, risky code, vulnerable dependencies) and a running page for accessibility and SEO. Each audit gives a score and a list of findings. You select findings and send them to an agent as one task, with a short list instead of the whole report.

![A security audit with a score of 40 out of 100: eleven findings sorted by severity, the first a leaked GitHub token shown masked, with its fix on the right](/_astro/agent-audits.BDn5_xFa_btVBA.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Audits** in the activity bar, or press `⌘7` (on Windows and Linux `Ctrl+7`), or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Audits**.

The view has three tabs: **Security**, **Accessibility (WCAG)** and **SEO**. A number next to a tab name is the count of findings of its last report.

## How to run an audit

[Section titled “How to run an audit”](#how-to-run-an-audit)

1. Select a project in the top bar.

2. Choose a tab. **Security** reads the files of the project. **Accessibility (WCAG)** and **SEO** read a running page.

3. For the two page tabs, check the **Page URL**. It starts as the **Dev-mode app URL** of the project, or the page open in the [Browser](/agent/browser/), or `http://localhost:5173`. The audit button in the Browser toolbar brings the current page here.

4. Press **Run audit**, or `Enter` in the URL field.

5. Wait for the report. Each tab keeps its own report.

| Tab                      | What it checks                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Security**             | Secrets in tracked files, risky code patterns, and known vulnerabilities of npm, PyPI and Composer dependencies from OSV.dev. Only files tracked by git are scanned, so a project outside git gives no findings |
| **Accessibility (WCAG)** | The page, in a hidden window, with axe-core. WCAG 2.2 AA is the target of the checks, and axe-core finds only part of the problems                                                                              |
| **SEO**                  | Title, description, headings, canonical link, Open Graph, structured data, images without `alt`, `robots.txt`, sitemap and broken internal links                                                                |

Every rule has its own page: see [Audit rules](/agent/audit-rules/). Dependency checks send only package names and versions to OSV.dev, never code. See [Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/).

## How to read a report

[Section titled “How to read a report”](#how-to-read-a-report)

The top of the report shows the score from 0 to 100, the target, the number of findings, the time, and the statistics of the audit (for example the number of files and dependencies). A report starts at 100 and every finding lowers it by its severity. The numbers are always written beside the ring.

* The severity buttons filter the list. Each shows how many findings it holds.
* The table is sorted from the most severe. A row shows the severity, the issue with its rule name, and the place: a file and line, or the page.
* Click a row to see the details on the right: the description, the **Fix** and, for a page, the element.
* **Open file** opens the file in the editor you chose in **Settings**. **Documentation** appears when the finding has a link, for example to the OSV entry.

## How to send findings to an agent

[Section titled “How to send findings to an agent”](#how-to-send-findings-to-an-agent)

1. Tick the findings in the first column. The box in the header, **Select all**, ticks all the findings of the current filter. For one finding use **Fix this** in its details.

2. Press **Fix with an agent (N)**. The dialog **Fix N findings** opens.

3. Choose the target: **New session** of an installed agent (the default agent is chosen) or a running session of the list.

4. Press **Send**. The app switches to the Agents view, on that session.

The agent gets a concise list of up to 40 findings: for each one its severity, title, place, the first line of the description and the proposed fix. It is asked to fix them from the most severe, to check that nothing breaks, to list what it fixed and what it did not, and to make no commit. A new session is titled **Fixes** and the kind of the audit. The message is written in Polish.

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

An audit of a local dev server always reports the rule `https`. That is expected: a dev address has no HTTPS.

* Run the three audits at once with the built-in pipeline **Three audits in parallel**, see [Pipelines](/agent/pipelines/).
* Fix the critical findings first. A leaked key must be revoked, not only removed from the code.
* axe-core does not replace a manual check: test keyboard use, focus order and alternative text by hand.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Audit rules](/agent/audit-rules/)Every rule of the three audits, with its severity.

[Pipelines](/agent/pipelines/)Run three audits in parallel with different agents.

[Accessibility](/agent/accessibility/)Accessibility of Skribly Agent itself.

[Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/)What audits send, and where.

# Browser

> The Browser view of Skribly Agent previews your app at phone, tablet and laptop widths, takes screenshots for agents and can share its tabs over CDP.

The **Browser** view shows your running app next to your work. You preview it at laptop, tablet and phone width, open the developer tools and take a screenshot an agent can read. The same view has tabs for Claude, Codex, Cursor and Gemini, each in its own profile. If you wish, you can share the browser with agents over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so they click and read what you see.

![The Browser view with a Preview tab on localhost, the device size buttons, DevTools, screenshot and Share in the toolbar](/_astro/agent-browser.CC4dcP0s_Z19SAR0.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Browser** in the activity bar on the left, or press `⌘8`, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Browser**.

On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` in place of `⌘`.

## Tabs and profiles

[Section titled “Tabs and profiles”](#tabs-and-profiles)

Each kind of tab has its own persistent profile, with its own cookies, sign-in and storage. Signing in to one does not mix with another, and the session survives a restart.

| Tab         | Start page                                               |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Preview** | The project’s dev URL, otherwise `http://localhost:5173` |
| Claude      | `https://claude.ai`                                      |
| Codex       | `https://chatgpt.com/codex`                              |
| Cursor      | `https://cursor.com/agents`                              |
| Gemini      | `https://gemini.google.com`                              |

* The **+** button opens the **New tab** menu. You can have several previews but only one tab for each agent. An address on claude.ai, chatgpt.com, openai.com, cursor.com or gemini.google.com always opens in the tab of its own profile.
* Tabs and their addresses are remembered between launches. The middle mouse button closes a tab.
* The preview page has no access to Node.js or to the app.

## How to preview your app

[Section titled “How to preview your app”](#how-to-preview-your-app)

1. Start your dev server in a terminal.

2. Open **Browser**. The **Preview** tab loads the dev URL of the project, or `http://localhost:5173`.

3. Use the buttons in the toolbar: back, forward and reload, then the width of the preview frame: **Full width**, laptop (1366), tablet (820) and phone (390).

4. Type a different address in the **Address** field if you need one.

What the **Address** field does with what you type:

| You type         | What opens              |
| ---------------- | ----------------------- |
| `localhost:3000` | `http://localhost:3000` |
| `example.com`    | `https://example.com`   |
| Anything else    | A search on DuckDuckGo  |

The last row is a network call to a service outside your computer. See [Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/).

## How to take a screenshot for the agent

[Section titled “How to take a screenshot for the agent”](#how-to-take-a-screenshot-for-the-agent)

1. Open the page you want the agent to see.

2. Press **Screenshot for the agent** in the toolbar. The visible tab is saved as a PNG.

3. Paste the path, which is already in the clipboard, into the agent’s terminal and ask it to look at the file.

With a project selected the file goes to `.skribly/shots/podglad-<date>.png` in the project, and `.skribly/` is excluded from git locally. Without a project it goes to the `shots` folder in the app’s data folder.

## What is in the toolbar

[Section titled “What is in the toolbar”](#what-is-in-the-toolbar)

| Button                            | What it does                                                                     |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Back, **Next**, **Refresh**       | Move through the tab’s history and reload it                                     |
| **Address**                       | The address field described above                                                |
| **Device**                        | Sets the width of the preview frame                                              |
| **Developer tools**               | Opens the tab’s developer tools                                                  |
| **Screenshot for the agent**      | Saves the visible tab as described above                                         |
| **WCAG / SEO audit of this page** | Audits the page; see [Audits](/agent/audits/)                                    |
| **Share**                         | Opens **Browser for agents**. It reads **Agents can see it** while sharing is on |

## Share the browser with agents

[Section titled “Share the browser with agents”](#share-the-browser-with-agents)

Skribly can open a Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) port, so that `chrome-devtools-mcp` or Playwright MCP control the tabs of this view. They click, fill in forms, read the console and the network, and take screenshots, while you watch the same thing. It is off by default.

1. Open **Settings**, section **Browser for agents**, and switch on **Share browser with agents**. Or press **Share** in the Browser view and then **Go to settings**.

2. Change the **Port** if you need to. The default is `9333`, and the allowed range is 1024 to 65535.

3. Restart Skribly. The port opens only when the app starts. Until then **Status** shows **requires restart**. When it is open, **Status** shows the address, for example `127.0.0.1:9333`.

4. Add the MCP server to your agent with a snippet from **MCP configuration**, and open the tab the agent should work with.

While sharing is on, the status bar shows `CDP 127.0.0.1:9333`.

The port listens only on `127.0.0.1`, but it accepts connections from any program on this computer. All tabs are then visible, including the signed-in Claude and Cursor profiles. Switch sharing on only while you work with agents.

| Setting                       | Value            | Default |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------- | ------- |
| **Share browser with agents** | On or off        | Off     |
| **Port**                      | 1024 to 65535    | `9333`  |
| Listens on                    | `127.0.0.1` only |         |

The section **MCP configuration** has a snippet for each of **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **Cursor**, **Gemini CLI** and **Playwright MCP**, with your port filled in. For Claude Code it is:

```bash
claude mcp add chrome-devtools -- npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest --browserUrl http://127.0.0.1:9333
```

Codex reads `~/.codex/config.toml`, Cursor `.cursor/mcp.json` or `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, and Gemini CLI `~/.gemini/settings.json`. Playwright MCP uses `--cdp-endpoint` in place of `--browserUrl`. Turn the servers on and off in [MCP servers](/agent/mcp/).

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Caution

A shared browser exposes every tab, including signed-in ones, to any program on this computer. Keep sharing off when you do not work with an agent.

* If the port is taken, choose another one in **Settings**, section **Browser for agents**, and restart. See [Troubleshooting](/agent/troubleshooting/#the-browser-port-is-in-use).
* Files you download in the Claude tab, such as an export from Claude Design, go to `Skribly Design` in your Downloads folder. See [Plugins and Claude Design](/agent/plugins/).

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Plugins and Claude Design](/agent/plugins/)Hand a Claude Design package to an agent.

[MCP servers](/agent/mcp/)Add and check the browser MCP servers of your agents.

[Audits](/agent/audits/)WCAG and SEO audits of a page.

[Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/)What the app contacts and what its switch covers.

# Changes and commits

> Stage and discard changes, read a side-by-side diff, get a commit message suggestion without a model, commit, switch branches, push, pull and open a pull request.

The **Changes** tab of the **Code & git** view shows what changed in the project: files in the index (staged) and files with working changes. From there you stage and discard files, read each diff, write a commit message, commit, switch branches, push, pull and open a pull request. The commit message suggestion needs no language model, and no commit made here carries an AI trailer.

![The Code & git view: the commit box with Suggest and Agent, staged files and changes on the left, and a side-by-side diff of CartDrawer.tsx](/_astro/agent-code-changes.CiUyqL1P_ZG3RjB.webp)

On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` wherever this page says `⌘`.

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Code & git** in the activity bar, or press `⌘4`, or choose **Code & git** in the command palette (`⌘K`).
* **Changes and commit** is the tab that opens first. Its icon shows the number of changed files.

The view refreshes itself every 8 seconds, while the window has focus, so changes made by agents show up. The refresh button in the panel head reloads at once. If the project is not a git repository, the tab says so; run `git init` in the terminal to start one.

## How to read and stage changes

[Section titled “How to read and stage changes”](#how-to-read-and-stage-changes)

1. Look at the two lists: **Staged (N)** and **Changes (N)**. A letter before each file tells its state: `A` added, `M` modified, `D` deleted, `R` renamed, `U` untracked, `!` conflict.

2. Click a file. A staged file opens as a side-by-side diff of **HEAD** against the index. A working file opens as a diff of the index against the disk. An untracked file opens in the editor, because it has nothing to compare with.

3. Press **Stage** next to a file (the plus) to move it to the index, or **Unstage** (the minus) to take it back. The buttons in the section headers do it for every file at once.

4. In the header of the diff, **Edit** opens the file in the editor, and **Add** or **Revert** stages or unstages it and closes the diff.

## How to discard changes

[Section titled “How to discard changes”](#how-to-discard-changes)

1. Press **Discard changes** next to a working file. For an untracked file the button is **Delete new file**. The button in the **Changes** header, **Discard all working changes**, takes every working file except conflicts.

2. Read the dialog. It lists the tracked files that return to their state in the index, and, in red, the new files that are deleted from the disk.

3. Confirm with **Discard changes**. This cannot be undone.

Staged files are not touched by a discard: unstage them first.

## How to commit

[Section titled “How to commit”](#how-to-commit)

1. Stage the files you want in the commit.

2. Press **Suggest**. The message field fills in, and under the buttons you see the template and where it came from, the reasons for the type and the scope, and clickable alternatives. Click one to use it instead.

3. Optional: press **Agent**. A headless agent reads the draft, the commit rules of the repository, the last 20 commit subjects and a summary of the staged diff, and returns an improved message. The button needs staged files and an installed agent with a headless mode (the default agent if it has one, otherwise the first that does). The agent cannot change files, and its answer is only a proposal in the field.

4. Edit the message, then press **Commit**, or press `⌘↩` in the field.

When nothing is staged, the commit button stages all changes, untracked files included, and commits them. The commit goes through `git commit`, and the message is always stripped of AI trailers, also one you typed by hand.

### What Suggest does

[Section titled “What Suggest does”](#what-suggest-does)

**Suggest** works from the staged files, or from all changes when nothing is staged. It spends no tokens. The steps, in order:

| Step           | Rule                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Template       | Taken from the **Commit template** field of the project settings. Without it, matched against the last 80 commit subjects (merges left out): `{type}({scope}): {subject}`, `{type}: {subject}`, `#{key} - {subject}`, `{key}: {subject}`, `[{key}] {subject}` or plain `{subject}`. The two Conventional Commits forms count together against the others; the scoped one wins on a tie. With fewer than 5 commits the default is used, and the reasons say so |
| Language       | Polish when more than 30% of the subjects contain Polish letters or typical Polish words. The **Commit language** field of the project settings forces Polish or English                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Capital letter | The subject starts with a capital when most of the history does, or when the template has `{key}`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Type           | From the branch if it starts with `feat`, `feature`, `fix`, `bugfix`, `hotfix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `chore`, `test`, `perf`, `ci` or `build` and `/` or `-`; else `docs` for documentation only, `test` for tests only, `ci` for CI files only, `build` for dependency and build files only, `feat` when at least half the files are new, `refactor` for deletions only, otherwise `fix`                                                                      |
| Scope          | In a monorepo, the package under `packages/`, `apps/`, `libs/`, `services/` or `modules/`. For one file, its name without the extension (up to 24 characters). For several, the deepest common folder, skipping generic names such as `src`, `app`, `lib`, `components` and `views`                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Key            | From a local task whose key is in the branch name, or from the branch itself (`ABC-123`, or a number of at least two digits). If the template needs a key and there is none, the reasons tell you                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Subject        | The title of that local task, else the words of the last part of the branch (at least two, without `feature`, `fix` and numbers), else a description of the files                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

The alternatives are the same subject in the forms `{type}({scope})`, `{type}` and `#{key}` (or plain when there is no key).

### What the Agent button reads

[Section titled “What the Agent button reads”](#what-the-agent-button-reads)

The agent is asked for a Conventional Commit message in English. Its answer loses every `Co-Authored-By` and “Generated with” line, and a `Signed-off-by` line unless you wrote the same one in the draft. It gets:

* The commit rules of the repository: the commit sections of `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` (also in `.github/` and `docs/`), a commitlint configuration and `.gitmessage`. Each source is cut to 1,800 characters and all together to 6,000. A file larger than 256 KB, or a link that leaves the project, is not read.
* The last 20 commit subjects, merges left out.
* A summary of the staged diff of up to 12,000 characters: first the statistics for every staged file, then hunks, source code before configuration, tests, documents and generated files. A note says how many hunks were left out.

## How to remove AI trailers from every commit

[Section titled “How to remove AI trailers from every commit”](#how-to-remove-ai-trailers-from-every-commit)

Press **Hook without AI trailers** at the bottom of the tab. It installs a `commit-msg` hook in the repository’s common git folder, so it works in all of its worktrees, and it also cleans the commits that agents make in a terminal.

The hook removes:

* `Co-Authored-By:` lines that name an agent as a whole word (`claude`, `anthropic`, `openai`, `codex`, `copilot`, `cursor`, `gemini`, `aider`, `devin ai`), the word `bot`, or a `noreply@` address;
* lines that start with `Generated with` or `Generated by` and an agent name;
* lines that start with 🤖.

The rest of the message stays. A human co-author is not removed, even if the name only contains an agent name inside a longer word. A `commit-msg` hook that was already there is set aside as `commit-msg.przed-skribly` and still runs after the cleanup. If `core.hooksPath` points elsewhere (husky, lefthook), git does not read this hook: add the cleanup to your own `commit-msg`.

## How to switch or create a branch

[Section titled “How to switch or create a branch”](#how-to-switch-or-create-a-branch)

1. Press the branch button at the top of the tab. The **Branches** dialog opens.

2. To create a branch, type its name (for example `feature/PROJ-12-search`) and press **Create** or `Enter`. It is created from the current one and checked out.

3. To switch, click a local branch. A branch that exists only on the remote is listed in grey; clicking it creates a local branch that tracks it.

The current branch is marked **current**.

## How to push, pull and open a pull request

[Section titled “How to push, pull and open a pull request”](#how-to-push-pull-and-open-a-pull-request)

1. Press the pull button (the arrow down). It runs `git pull --ff-only`; the tooltip shows how many commits are waiting.

2. Press the push button (the arrow up). It runs `git push -u origin HEAD`, and the number next to it is how many commits are ahead.

3. After a push of a branch that is not the base branch, a bar offers **Create PR**. It runs `gh pr create` with the title and text of the last commit, without agent trailers, and the project’s base branch as the target when one is set.

4. When the branch already has an open pull request, the bar shows its number with a button that opens it in the browser.

Pull requests need the GitHub CLI (`gh`) and a GitHub remote. Without `gh` the bar offers **Install gh**; without a login it offers **Log in to GitHub**. Push and pull use the git setup you already have (SSH keys, a credential manager): the app passes no token.

Note

With **No network calls by the app** switched on in **Settings**, push, pull and the pull request bar are blocked.

## What is on the screen

[Section titled “What is on the screen”](#what-is-on-the-screen)

| Part                            | What it does                                                                          |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Branch button                   | Opens **Branches**                                                                    |
| Pull and push buttons           | `git pull --ff-only` and `git push -u origin HEAD`                                    |
| Message field                   | The commit message; `⌘↩` commits                                                      |
| **Suggest**                     | A message from the changes, the branch and the history, with reasons and alternatives |
| **Agent**                       | An agent improves the message, read-only                                              |
| **Commit**                      | Commits the staged files                                                              |
| **Staged (N)**, **Changes (N)** | The two file lists                                                                    |
| **Hook without AI trailers**    | Installs the `commit-msg` hook                                                        |

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

Stage related files only, then press **Suggest**: the type and the scope come from the staged files, so a small commit gets a precise message.

* Name branches `feature/ABC-123-short-title`: the type, the key and the subject all come from the name.
* Always read an Agent message before you commit. It is a proposal.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Review notes](/agent/review/)Note lines of a diff and send them to an agent.

[History](/agent/history/)The graph of all branches, with commit details.

[Editor and files](/agent/code/)The same view as an editor.

[Worktrees](/agent/worktrees/)Every worktree of your projects and its state.

# The skribly command

> Control panes and agents of Skribly Agent from outside the window with the skribly command - targets, every command, exit codes, recipes for reviewers and parallel worktrees, and safety.

The `skribly` command lets agents, scripts and you control panes from outside the window. An agent can start a reviewer next to itself, wait for it and read the result. The same operations are offered to agents as MCP tools by [the Skribly MCP server](/agent/skribly-mcp/), which is started with `skribly mcp`.

## How it works

[Section titled “How it works”](#how-it-works)

* A control API runs inside the app and listens only on `127.0.0.1`, on a random free port.
* The port and a random token are written to `~/.skribly/control.json`, readable only by you. Requests without a valid token get `401`. The `SKRIBLY_CONTROL` variable can point to another file.
* `skribly` is a small script without dependencies. The installed command runs it inside the Skribly app in a mode without a window, so a separate Node.js is not needed.
* It works only while the app is running.
* A call from a Skribly pane passes that pane and its folder, so `current` and the default project mean the pane you are calling from.
* Sessions started this way appear in the **Agents** view like any other.

## How to turn it on

[Section titled “How to turn it on”](#how-to-turn-it-on)

1. Open **Settings → Sessions & control → Local control API**. It is on by default; the badge shows the port.

2. Under **skribly command**, press **Install**. The command goes to `~/.local/bin/skribly` on macOS and Linux and to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Skribly\bin` on Windows. If that folder is not in your `PATH`, Skribly says what to add, for example `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` in `~/.zshrc`.

3. Optionally install the **“skribly” skill for agents** in a project. It teaches Claude Code and Codex when and how to delegate work.

## Targets

[Section titled “Targets”](#targets)

Commands that act on an existing pane take a target.

| Target     | Example      | Notes                                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Agent name | `reviewer`   | Given at start (lower case, letters, digits, `_` and `-`, up to 32 characters) and shown as an `@name` badge in the pane. `pane rename` gives a name later |
| Pane id    | `3f2c9a1e-…` | At least the first 4 characters. From `pane list` or `agent list`                                                                                          |
| `current`  | `current`    | The pane the command was called from, only inside a Skribly terminal                                                                                       |

`--kind` takes `claude`, `codex`, `cursor`, `gemini`, `opencode`, `copilot`, `aider`, `amp`, `droid`, `qwen`, `goose`, `crush`, `kimi`, or `custom:<id>` for a custom agent from Settings. `--project` takes a project name, id or path. Timeouts are in seconds.

## Commands

[Section titled “Commands”](#commands)

| Command                                                                                                                                    | What it does                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `skribly status`                                                                                                                           | Number of panes and agents, and their states                                                          |
| `skribly workspace list`                                                                                                                   | Projects, their worktrees and the panes in each, with one rolled-up state                             |
| `skribly pane list`                                                                                                                        | All panes, shells and agents                                                                          |
| `skribly pane create [name] [--kind shell\|<agent>] [--project P\|--cwd D] [--title T] [--prompt X] [--worktree BRANCH] [--machine M]`     | Opens a new pane                                                                                      |
| `skribly pane run <target> <command…>`                                                                                                     | Types a shell command and Enter                                                                       |
| `skribly pane read <target> [--lines N]`                                                                                                   | Reads the screen and the last lines as text                                                           |
| `skribly pane wait-output <target> <regex> [--timeout S] [--new]`                                                                          | Waits until the output matches; `--new` looks only at output after the call                           |
| `skribly pane rename <target> [name]`                                                                                                      | Names a pane for the API                                                                              |
| `skribly pane close <target>`                                                                                                              | Closes a pane                                                                                         |
| `skribly agent list`                                                                                                                       | Agents and their states: `working`, `blocked`, `done`, `idle`, `exited`                               |
| `skribly agent start <name> --kind <agent> [--project P\|--cwd D] [--prompt X] [--worktree BRANCH] [--base REF] [--machine M] [--title T]` | Starts a named agent in a new pane; with `--worktree`, in a worktree of that branch                   |
| `skribly agent prompt <target> <text…> [--wait] [--timeout S] [--lines N]`                                                                 | Sends a message; with `--wait` it waits for the end of the turn and returns the screen                |
| `skribly agent read <target> [--lines N]`                                                                                                  | Reads the agent’s screen                                                                              |
| `skribly agent wait <target> [--until done,idle,blocked\|finished] [--timeout S]`                                                          | Waits for one of the states; the default is `done,idle,blocked,exited`, and `finished` means the same |
| `skribly agent explain <target>`                                                                                                           | Shows why the agent is in its state: the rule, the process and the screen                             |
| `skribly agent stop <target>`                                                                                                              | Closes the agent’s pane, which ends the agent                                                         |
| `skribly worktree list [--project P]`                                                                                                      | Lists a project’s worktrees                                                                           |
| `skribly worktree create <branch> [--base B] [--project P]`                                                                                | Creates a worktree; an existing branch is checked out, a new one starts from the base or `HEAD`       |
| `skribly worktree remove <path\|branch> [--force] [--project P]`                                                                           | Removes the worktree folder and keeps the branch                                                      |
| `skribly notify <title> [body…]`                                                                                                           | Sends a system notification                                                                           |
| `skribly mcp [--allow-writes] [--project P]`                                                                                               | Runs the MCP server on standard input and output; see [the Skribly MCP server](/agent/skribly-mcp/)   |
| `skribly --help`                                                                                                                           | Prints the help                                                                                       |

## Output and exit codes

[Section titled “Output and exit codes”](#output-and-exit-codes)

Every command prints JSON to standard output. `--text` with `read` and `explain` prints plain text. Errors go to standard error as `{"error": "…"}`.

| Code  | Meaning                                                                                  |
| ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `0`   | Success                                                                                  |
| `1`   | Error, such as an unknown target                                                         |
| `2`   | Bad usage or no connection: Skribly is not running, the API is off or the token is stale |
| `124` | The timeout was exceeded in `wait`, `wait-output` or `prompt --wait`                     |

## Recipes

[Section titled “Recipes”](#recipes)

### A reviewer next to the implementer

[Section titled “A reviewer next to the implementer”](#a-reviewer-next-to-the-implementer)

```bash
skribly agent start reviewer --kind claude --prompt "Review the changes from git diff. List issues from most severe, with file:line."
skribly agent wait reviewer --until done --timeout 600
skribly agent read reviewer --lines 60 --text
```

Called from a Skribly pane, the reviewer starts in that pane’s project. You see it in the pane next to the implementer and can answer it. For the next turn, one command is enough:

```bash
skribly agent prompt reviewer "Check again after the fixes" --wait --timeout 600 --lines 40
```

### Parallel worktrees

[Section titled “Parallel worktrees”](#parallel-worktrees)

Each agent gets its own folder and branch, so they do not overwrite each other’s files.

```bash
skribly agent start impl-api --kind codex --worktree feature/api-export --prompt "Build the CSV export endpoint per SPEC.md"
skribly agent start impl-ui --kind claude --worktree feature/ui-export --prompt "Build the export button per SPEC.md"
skribly agent wait impl-api --until finished --timeout 1800
skribly agent wait impl-ui --until finished --timeout 1800
```

Combine the results with a normal merge, then clean up with `skribly worktree remove feature/api-export`. See [Worktrees](/agent/worktrees/).

### Wait, then react

[Section titled “Wait, then react”](#wait-then-react)

`blocked` means the agent is asking for permission or a choice.

```bash
skribly agent wait impl-api --until done,blocked --timeout 900
skribly agent explain impl-api --text
skribly agent read impl-api --lines 30 --text
skribly agent prompt impl-api "1"
```

### Wait for a shell command

[Section titled “Wait for a shell command”](#wait-for-a-shell-command)

```bash
skribly pane create tests --kind shell
skribly pane run tests npm test
skribly pane wait-output tests "Tests:.*(passed|failed)" --timeout 300 --new
```

## Safety

[Section titled “Safety”](#safety)

Caution

Other system users cannot read `control.json`, but any process of your own user can, and with the token it controls your agents. The `skribly` command itself never asks before it acts. If you do not use the API, turn it off with its switch in **Settings**.

The ports the app opens are listed in [Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/#ports).

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[The Skribly MCP server](/agent/skribly-mcp/)The same control as MCP tools, read-only by default.

[Agents and sessions](/agent/sessions/)Sessions started by the command appear here.

[Worktrees](/agent/worktrees/)Separate folders and branches for parallel agents.

[Keyboard shortcuts](/agent/shortcuts/)Pane, app and editor keys.

# Editor and files

> The Code & git view of Skribly Agent works as an editor: a file tree, tabs, quick open, search in files, Monaco, saving, agent actions on code and a terminal.

The **Code & git** view is an editor built for work next to agents. It has a file tree, tabs, quick open, search in files, the Monaco editor (the one of VS Code), a terminal in the bottom panel, and a way to send selected code to an agent. When an agent changes a file you have open, the editor shows it. The same view holds [changes and commits](/agent/changes/), [review notes](/agent/review/) and the [history graph](/agent/history/).

On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` wherever this page says `⌘`.

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Code & git** in the activity bar on the left, or
* press `⌘4`, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Code & git**.

The view works on the project selected in the top bar. Without a project it asks you to select one. The left panel has four tabs, shown as icons: **Changes and commit** (open by default), **Files**, **Search in files** and **History**.

## How to open a file

[Section titled “How to open a file”](#how-to-open-a-file)

1. Open the **Files** tab. The tree lists the files git knows (tracked and untracked, without ignored ones). Outside a repository it scans the folder instead and skips `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`, `out`, `build`, `.next`, `vendor`, `.venv`, `target` and similar. The tree holds at most 20,000 files.

2. Click a file. It opens in a tab above the editor. Several files can be open at once, and the path above the editor shows where the file is in the tree.

3. Close a tab with its **x**, or with `⌘W` while the focus is in the editor. Elsewhere `⌘W` stays the window shortcut. A tab with unsaved changes asks before it closes.

A file larger than 2 MB, and a binary file, is not opened: the view says **File is too large or binary** and points you to your own editor. The **Open in external editor** button above the editor opens the file in the editor chosen in **Settings**.

Paths are guarded: the view refuses to read or write outside the project folder.

## How to find a file or a text

[Section titled “How to find a file or a text”](#how-to-find-a-file-or-a-text)

1. Press `⌘P` for **Quick open file**. Type part of a name; the match is fuzzy, and recent files come first. Add `:123` to the name to jump to line 123.

2. Move with `↑` and `↓` (also `Ctrl+N` and `Ctrl+P`), open with `Enter`, close with `Esc`.

3. To search inside files, press `⌘⇧F`, or open the **Search in files** tab. Type the text; the search starts while you type, and `Enter` runs it at once.

4. Use the buttons in the field for **Match case** and **Regular expression**, and the file filter for patterns such as `*.ts, src/**, !*.test.ts`. A click on a result opens the file with the match selected.

The search shows up to 2,000 matches and says so when it reaches the limit. It uses ripgrep from your `PATH` or from an installed VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf or VSCodium. Without ripgrep it scans text files up to 1 MB in the app and skips folders such as `node_modules` and `dist`.

## How to edit and save

[Section titled “How to edit and save”](#how-to-edit-and-save)

1. Click in the editor and type. An unsaved file shows a dot in its tab and **unsaved** in the bar below the editor.

2. Press `⌘S` or the **Save** button. The button is off while nothing changed.

3. Press `Ctrl+G` (or the cursor position in the bar below the editor) to go to a line.

The editor takes its colours from the day or night theme of the app. The bar below it shows the cursor line and column, the selection size, the language, UTF-8 and the line ending.

## Files that an agent changes

[Section titled “Files that an agent changes”](#files-that-an-agent-changes)

The view checks the open file every two seconds, and when the window gets focus, while the window is visible. It also refreshes the file list and the changes every 8 seconds.

* If you have no unsaved changes, the file reloads by itself. The cursor and scroll stay in place unless the change is where they are.
* If you have unsaved changes, a bar appears: **The file was changed on disk (e.g. by an agent), and the editor has unsaved changes.** Choose **Reload** to take the disk version or **Keep mine** to keep yours.
* If the file is gone, the bar says **The file no longer exists on disk.** Save to recreate it, or close the tab.

## How to send code to an agent

[Section titled “How to send code to an agent”](#how-to-send-code-to-an-agent)

1. Select the code you mean. With no selection the whole file counts.

2. Open the **Agent** menu above the editor, or right-click and choose a command of the **Agent:** group. **Ask the agent…** also has the shortcut `⌘⇧I`.

3. In the dialog pick the target: a running session (the ones of this project come first) or **New session: \<agent>** of an installed agent. The last choice is remembered.

4. Read the prompt in **Command** and edit it if you want. **restore** brings back the generated one.

5. Press **Send** (`⌘↩`). With a running session you can tick **Go to the agent after sending** to open the Agents view.

| Action             | What the prompt asks the agent to do                                                     |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Ask the agent…** | Your own question about the selected code                                                |
| **Explain**        | Say briefly what the code does and why; change no files                                  |
| **Fix**            | Find and fix bugs, change only what is needed, describe the fix                          |
| **Write tests**    | Write tests in the framework and style of the project, then run them                     |
| **Review**         | Review bugs, edge cases, security, speed and clarity, with line numbers; change no files |

The prompt always names the file and the lines (`path:from-to`). A selection of up to 40 lines and 2,400 characters goes into the prompt as it is. A longer one is left to the agent, which reads it from disk. If the file has unsaved changes, the code from the editor goes into the prompt instead (up to 150 lines and 8,000 characters), because the agent cannot see it on disk, and the dialog says so.

## How to use the terminal

[Section titled “How to use the terminal”](#how-to-use-the-terminal)

Press `` Ctrl+` `` (also on macOS) or the terminal button in the panel head. A shell opens at the bottom, in the project folder. Drag its top edge, or use `↑` and `↓` on the edge, to change its height. **New shell** restarts it, and **Hide panel** closes the panel.

The project has one such shell: showing and hiding the panel starts no new one. It does not appear in the [Agents view](/agent/terminals/), and it is not kept after you quit the app.

Note

On Windows and Linux, `Ctrl+P` and `Ctrl+G` belong to the shell while the focus is in the terminal.

## Shortcuts

[Section titled “Shortcuts”](#shortcuts)

| Shortcut     | Action                              |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| `⌘4`         | Open the view                       |
| `⌘P`         | Quick open file                     |
| `⌘⇧F`        | Search in files                     |
| `⌘S`         | Save the file                       |
| `⌘W`         | Close the tab (focus in the editor) |
| `Ctrl+G`     | Go to line                          |
| `⌘⇧I`        | Ask the agent about the selection   |
| `` Ctrl+` `` | Show or hide the terminal           |

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

Drag the edge of the left panel to change its width (between 240 and 720 pixels; a double click restores it). The width is remembered.

* Select a few lines rather than the whole file when you ask an agent: a short selection costs fewer tokens and gives a sharper answer.
* Use **Review** on a selection to get comments without any change to your files.

# Dashboard

> The Dashboard of Skribly Agent: start actions, detected agents, the Getting started list, counters, repository activity, the token chart, projects and recent commits.

The Dashboard is the first view. It sums up your work in one page: how many agents work and how many wait for you, your commits, your token use and your projects. You use it to start work and to see where things stand.

![The Dashboard at night: Run agent, My tasks and Add project, the detected agents, the Getting started checklist, four counters and the repository activity](/_astro/agent-dashboard.B-bd5UjR_Z1OjYe0.webp)

![The same Dashboard in the day theme](/_astro/agent-dashboard-light.B7FQSym8_Z1q2vDG.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Dashboard** in the activity bar on the left, or press `⌘1`, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Dashboard**.

Shortcuts on this site use `⌘`. On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` instead.

## What is on the page

[Section titled “What is on the page”](#what-is-on-the-page)

| Part                         | What it shows or does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Hero                         | The greeting and three actions: **Run agent** opens the Agents view with a new session of the first installed agent (a plain shell when none is installed), **My tasks** opens [Tasks](/agent/tasks/), **Add project** asks for a folder                             |
| Detected agents              | One chip per agent. An installed agent shows its name and version on hover. A missing one is dimmed; clicking it starts its installation                                                                                                                             |
| **Getting started**          | The setup list described on [First run](/agent/first-run/). It is hidden once you close it                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Counters                     | **agents working now**, **waiting for your decision** (click it for the Agents view), **tasks in progress** (click it for Tasks) and **Your commits in 7 days**                                                                                                      |
| **Repository activity**      | Your commits and, when you have connected Git accounts, their calendars. Ranges: **14 days**, **3 mo.** and **year**. The summary gives the days in a row, the longest streak, the total of this year and this week. The refresh button scans the repositories again |
| **Agent tokens — 14 days**   | A chart of tokens per day. Group it by **Kind**, **Agent** or **Model**, and switch the counted kinds: **Input**, **Output**, **Cache write**, **Cache read**. **Board** opens the [token use board](/agent/usage/). **How this is counted** explains the sources    |
| **Most active repositories** | The repositories with the most of your commits in the chosen range                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Projects**                 | Every project with its number of sessions. Click one to select it and open the Code view. **Add** adds a project                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Recent commits**           | Your latest commits of the last 14 days from all projects, with their hash, subject and age. Click one to open its project in the Code view                                                                                                                          |

The activity counts your commits from all branches of your projects and of the repositories in the folders you chose, under all your git email addresses. When it finds none, the card says which addresses it searched for and suggests connecting a GitHub or GitLab account. You connect accounts in **Settings → Git accounts**.

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

The counters and the lists load again when you add a project, start or close a session, or when the activity is refreshed.

* A missing agent chip is the shortest way to install an agent: it opens the install progress in the app. The commands are on [Supported agents](/agent/agents/).
