# MCP servers

> The MCP servers tab of Skribly Agent lists the servers of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini, switches them, checks that one answers and copies it.

The **MCP servers** tab, in **Plugins & MCP**, lists the MCP servers that Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini have configured, for you and for the open project. You can switch a server off without destroying its configuration, add one to several agents at once, check that it really starts and answers, and copy an entry from one agent to another. Nothing runs by itself and no secret is ever shown.

This page is about the servers the agents use. Skribly Agent has an MCP server of its own, `skribly mcp`, which is described in [The Agent’s own MCP server](/agent/skribly-mcp/).

![The MCP servers tab: the servers of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor Agent and Gemini CLI with their scope, transport, on and off switches and the check, copy, folder and delete buttons](/_astro/agent-mcp.DmPfvzuG_Z1WXIFT.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Plugins & MCP** in the activity bar on the left and choose the **MCP servers** tab, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Plugins & MCP**.

On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` in place of `⌘`. The view has no number shortcut: `⌘1` to `⌘9` stay with the first nine views.

## The list

[Section titled “The list”](#the-list)

There is one card per agent, with the number of its servers. A row shows the name, the scope, the transport and the command or address. The scope is **everywhere**, **project (repo)** or **project (only me)**. The transport is `stdio` for a program the agent starts, or `http` or `sse` for an address.

| Agent       | Read from                                                                     |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude.json` (everywhere, and per project) and `.mcp.json` in the project |
| Codex       | `~/.codex/config.toml`, the `[mcp_servers.NAME]` sections                     |
| Cursor      | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` and `.cursor/mcp.json` in the project                    |
| Gemini CLI  | `~/.gemini/settings.json` and `.gemini/settings.json` in the project          |

Each row has a switch and four buttons: the check, the copy, **Show file** (it opens the file the entry comes from) and **Delete server**. The agent sees a change in a new session.

## How to switch a server off and on

[Section titled “How to switch a server off and on”](#how-to-switch-a-server-off-and-on)

Press the switch of the row. Agents have no common “disabled” flag, so Skribly handles each format in its own way, and switching on restores exactly the same configuration.

| Server                                  | Switching off                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Codex                                   | `enabled = false` in its section of `config.toml`                                                                                                                                 |
| Claude Code, `.mcp.json` of the project | The name goes to `disabledMcpjsonServers` in `.claude/settings.local.json`. The `.mcp.json` from the repository stays untouched                                                   |
| Claude Code, everywhere or only me      | The configuration is saved in Skribly’s own stash (`mcp-stash.json` in the data folder) and the server is removed with `claude mcp remove`, or from the file when there is no CLI |
| Cursor and Gemini                       | The same stash, and the entry is removed from the file                                                                                                                            |

Servers in the stash show on the list as off. Skribly also reads switch-offs made by hand.

## How to add a server

[Section titled “How to add a server”](#how-to-add-a-server)

1. Press **Add MCP server**. Pick a preset (Chrome DevTools, Playwright, Context7, Skribly, Skribly with writes, Figma (Dev Mode), Sentry, Atlassian or Linear) or fill the form in yourself.

2. Tick the agents in **To agent**. Choose the scope. Codex always saves to the user configuration, and the dialog says so.

3. Give a **Name** (letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`) and choose the **Transport**: `stdio` (a local program), HTTP or SSE.

4. For a program give the command and the **Arguments**. For an address give the address. Add environment variables (`KEY=value`, one per line) or, for an address, headers (`Name: value`, one per line).

5. Save. A message lists the files that were written.

Skribly writes the entry in each agent’s own format: `claude mcp add-json` for Claude Code (or the file when there is no CLI), a new `[mcp_servers.<name>]` section for Codex, `mcpServers` in `mcp.json` for Cursor and in `settings.json` for Gemini.

The **Skribly with writes** preset starts `skribly mcp --allow-writes`. Every change it makes then asks you in the app first.

Caution

Prefer a reference to an environment variable over a value typed into the form. A value you type is written into the agent’s file as it is. See [Extensions](/agent/extensions/) for entries that keep only the variable’s name.

## How to check a server

[Section titled “How to check a server”](#how-to-check-a-server)

The check shows what it would do before it does anything.

![The dialog Check server playwright: the command and folder that were started, and the answer in 550 ms with five tools](/_astro/agent-mcp-test.DoD5l3KR_1LkLPA.webp)

1. Press the check button on the row. Switch the server on first: a server that is off is not started.

2. A dialog shows what the test would do. For a program it shows the command with its arguments and the folder it would start in. For an address it shows the address. Environment variables and headers appear by name only, never by value. Nothing has started yet.

3. Press **Run the test**, or `Esc` to cancel. Skribly starts the program as its agent would (or sends the request to the address), does the first handshake (`initialize`), asks for the list of tools (`tools/list`) and stops the program with everything it started.

4. Read the result. The time limit is 20 seconds. A badge stays on the row until you reload the list.

| Result                                                                     | Meaning                                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **running**, **Answered in** N ms with the number of tools and their names | The server started and answered                                       |
| No answer within the time limit                                            | The server took longer than 20 seconds                                |
| The server ended before it answered                                        | The dialog gives the exit code and the last lines the program printed |
| Something that is not an MCP message                                       | The program prints text that is not JSON-RPC                          |
| The command was not found                                                  | The command is not in `PATH`                                          |
| The server wants a login                                                   | An address answered HTTP 401 or 403, or a login or token is needed    |

Secrets are hidden everywhere in the dialog: values of variables and headers, `user:password@` in an address, query values, and the value after `--token`, `--api-key` or `--password` appear as `•••`, and the same values are cut out of error text. A server from a project file may use only the variables its own entry declares, so a cloned repository cannot send a variable of yours to an address.

With **No network calls by the app** on, a server with a remote address is not contacted, and the dialog says so. An address on this computer (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`) is still tested. A program you start with a command is not stopped by the switch, and what that program does on the network is its own traffic. See [Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/).

## How to copy a server to another agent

[Section titled “How to copy a server to another agent”](#how-to-copy-a-server-to-another-agent)

1. Press the copy button on the row.

2. Choose **To agent** and the **Scope**. Codex has only the user file, Cursor and Gemini have everywhere and project, and only Claude Code has **project (only me)**.

3. Read the dialog. It shows the file that would change, the one entry that would be written in that agent’s format with the values of variables and headers hidden, and the name of the backup. A reference such as `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` stays visible and is converted to the other agent’s syntax. If the agent has a server of that name already, nothing is changed.

4. Press **Write this entry**. Skribly copies the file next to itself as `NAME.skribly-backup-DATE`, readable only by you, and adds the entry. Other entries stay as they are, and a JSON file that cannot be read is never touched.

## How to delete a server

[Section titled “How to delete a server”](#how-to-delete-a-server)

Press **Delete server** on the row and confirm. The entry is removed from the file (for Codex the whole section) and from Skribly’s stash. Delete cannot be undone, so copy the entry first if you may want it back.

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

Run the check after you add a server. A server that starts but lists no tools, or fails on a login, is easier to spot here than inside an agent session.

* Use the folder button to open the file and see exactly what the agent reads.
* Keep project servers under **project (only me)** while you try them, and move them to **project (repo)** when the team should have them.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[The Agent's own MCP server](/agent/skribly-mcp/)skribly mcp: what other agents can read and change in Skribly Agent.

[Extensions](/agent/extensions/)MCP entries kept per agent or technology, with the names of variables only.

[Plugins and Claude Design](/agent/plugins/)Claude Code plugins, Claude Design to code and the Cursor tab.

[Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/)What the no-network switch covers.

# Pipelines

> A pipeline in Skribly Agent runs several agents on one goal, stage by stage, passing results through handoff.md; build your own, run it and follow it on a graph.

A pipeline is several agents, from different vendors if you like, working toward one goal. Steps of one stage run in parallel, later stages wait for earlier ones, and results pass through a file, `handoff.md`, instead of through you. Use a pipeline when the work has a natural order: plan, do, review.

![The Pipelines view: built-in pipelines and recent runs on the left, a running Plan, execution and review pipeline on a graph, and its steps on the right](/_astro/agent-pipelines.CvDBO-NR_Z1DjvJY.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Pipelines** in the activity bar, or press `⌘5` (on Windows and Linux `Ctrl+5`), or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Pipelines**.

The left side lists the pipelines and **Recent runs**, the middle shows the graph, and the right side shows the steps of the run or the details of the step you click.

## How a run works

[Section titled “How a run works”](#how-a-run-works)

1. The app creates `.skribly/runs/<id>/handoff.md` in the project, with a header and your goal. `.skribly/` is added to `.git/info/exclude`.
2. For each stage, in order, it starts all steps of the stage at once. A step is a headless agent in the project folder. It gets the role and the prompt of the step, the goal of the whole job, the current `handoff.md` (the last 16,000 characters) and a request for a concise answer, because the answer goes to the next agent.
3. After a stage, the answers of its steps are appended to `handoff.md` as sections named `## Etap N: <role> (<agent>)`.
4. If a step fails (an error and no answer), the run ends as failed and the steps that did not start are skipped.
5. **Stop** interrupts the working agents and the run ends as stopped.

A step marked **modifies files** may edit: Claude runs with `acceptEdits`, Codex with `--full-auto`. Without it the step is read-only: Claude in `plan` mode, Codex with `--sandbox read-only`. An agent gets only the result of the earlier steps, not their whole conversation. That saves tokens and lets you combine vendors.

## Built-in pipelines

[Section titled “Built-in pipelines”](#built-in-pipelines)

| Pipeline                      | Steps                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Plan → execution → review** | 1: Planner (Claude, read-only) → 2: Implementer (Codex, modifies files, runs the project checks) → 3: Reviewer (Claude, read-only: reviews `git diff` and proposes a commit message) |
| **Three audits in parallel**  | 1: Security (Claude), accessibility against WCAG 2.2 AA (Gemini) and SEO (Codex) in parallel → 2: Coordinator (Claude) merges the results into one fix plan                          |
| **Fix, tests, documentation** | 1: Fix (Codex) → 2: Tests (Claude, runs only the tests the change affects) → 3: Documentation (Gemini updates `.docs/` and the README)                                               |

The built-in pipelines are listed until you save your own. From the first save the list comes from `pipelines.json` in the app’s data directory.

## How to run a pipeline

[Section titled “How to run a pipeline”](#how-to-run-a-pipeline)

1. Select a project in the top bar, and a pipeline in the list.

2. Type the goal in the field, for example “Add report export to CSV with filters like in the table view”.

3. Press **Run**, or `Enter` in the field.

4. Follow the graph. A node shows the state of its step. Click a node to see the prompt and the result of the step on the right.

5. When the run is over, press **Show handoff.md** to see the handoff file in the file manager.

**Run** is off while the goal is empty, no project is selected, or an agent of the pipeline is missing. The message **Not detected: …** over the graph names the agent: install it in **Settings → Agents** or change the agent of the step. While a run works, **Run** becomes **Stop**. Click a run under **Recent runs** to see it again. The last 30 runs are kept (`runs.json` in the data directory), and the list shows 12.

## How to create or edit a pipeline

[Section titled “How to create or edit a pipeline”](#how-to-create-or-edit-a-pipeline)

1. Press the plus in the head of the list (**New pipeline**), or select a pipeline and press **Duplicate** or **Edit**.

2. Type a **Name** and a **Description**.

3. Add steps with **Add step**. Each step has the fields below.

4. Press **Save**. **Save** is off without a name or without a step.

| Field              | Meaning                                                                            |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Stage**          | A number from 1. Steps with the same number run in parallel                        |
| **Role**           | For example “Planner” or “Tests”. It goes into the prompt as the role of the agent |
| **Agent**          | The agent that does the step                                                       |
| **modifies files** | Whether the agent may edit files                                                   |
| Prompt             | What the agent should do                                                           |
| **Delete step**    | Removes the step                                                                   |

On the graph every step of a stage connects to every step of the next stage. **Delete** in the toolbar removes the whole pipeline.

## How to arrange the graph

[Section titled “How to arrange the graph”](#how-to-arrange-the-graph)

* Drag a node to move it. Drag an edge of the node to resize it. Positions and sizes snap to a small grid.
* With a node focused (`Tab`), the arrow keys move it by one grid step and `Shift` with the arrows resizes it. `Enter` shows the step’s details. Double click expands the whole prompt of the node.
* The graph controls zoom in, zoom out and fit the graph to the window.
* **Reset layout** puts every node back in its computed place. It is off until you have moved something.

Moving or resizing a node only changes where it is drawn. It does not change the stage or the order of the run. The layout is saved with the pipeline, so it survives a restart.

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Caution

Steps that modify files in the same stage work in the same folder and can get in each other’s way. Put them in separate stages.

* End with a reviewer or a coordinator step that gathers the results into one list.
* Agents without a JSON mode answer in plain text. That is enough for the handoff.
* Pipelines send the agent’s prompt to the vendor of that agent, like any session. Read [Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/) for what the app itself sends.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Audits](/agent/audits/)Security, WCAG and SEO audits, with Fix with an agent.

[Supported agents](/agent/agents/)Which agents have a headless mode.

[Terminals and sessions](/agent/terminals/)Sessions, chat mode and handing off work.

# Plan

> The Plan view of Skribly Agent counts the Markdown checkboxes of your plan files, lists the open items and hands one to the Code view or to an agent.

The **Plan** view shows the plan a project keeps as Markdown checkboxes: a `TODO.md`, a `.docs/TODO.md`, a folder of step files. It counts what is done and what is open per file and per heading, lists the open items with a search, and hands an item to the Code view or to an agent. It only reads the files: it never ticks a box and never writes to a plan file.

![The Plan view in the day theme: totals of 10 done out of 26 at the top, five plan files with their progress bars on the left and sixteen open items with copy and hand-off buttons on the right](/_astro/agent-plan.CnlQRG5Y_ZBE4G0.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Plan** in the activity bar on the left (the icon with a checked list), or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Plan**.

The view has no number shortcut: `⌘1` to `⌘9` stay with the first nine views.

## How to hand an open item to an agent

[Section titled “How to hand an open item to an agent”](#how-to-hand-an-open-item-to-an-agent)

1. Open **Plan** and find the item under **Open items**. Type in **Search the open items** to filter by text, file or heading, or pick one file in the list next to it.

2. Press **Hand to an agent** next to the item. A dialog shows a prompt with the item, its file, line and heading.

3. Edit the prompt, then choose a running session of the project or a new session of an installed agent.

4. Press **Send** (`⌘↩`). Nothing is sent before you press it.

## How to change where the view looks

[Section titled “How to change where the view looks”](#how-to-change-where-the-view-looks)

1. Press **Plan paths** at the top of the view.

2. Write one pattern per line, relative to the project folder: `*` is any name inside one folder, `**` is any number of folders.

3. Press **Save**. The list is kept in the project’s settings. **Restore defaults** brings back the four default patterns.

| Pattern              | What it finds                                                  |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TODO.md`            | The to-do file at the top of the project (default)             |
| `.docs/TODO.md`      | The to-do file of the docs folder (default)                    |
| `.docs/plan/**/*.md` | Every Markdown file of the plan folder, at any depth (default) |
| `docs/plan/**/*.md`  | The same for a `docs` folder (default)                         |

A pattern that would leave the project folder (`../notes.md`, `/etc/…`, `~/…`, `C:\…`) is refused and named in the view. A symbolic link that points out of the project folder is not followed. Folders such as `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist` and `build` are skipped.

## What counts as an item

[Section titled “What counts as an item”](#what-counts-as-an-item)

An item is a list entry that starts with a checkbox:

```md
## Release 1.5


- [x] Move the cart to the new price helpers
- [ ] Write the release notes
  - [ ] Ask for a review


1. [x] Numbered lists count too
```

* `[ ]` is open; `[x]` and `[X]` are done. Bullets `-`, `*`, `+` and numbered lists (`1.` or `1)`) all count, at any depth.
* An item belongs to the nearest heading above it. A heading without items is left out.
* A line inside a code block, an HTML comment or the front matter is not an item, even if it looks like one.
* A file that is not saved as UTF-8, or is larger than 4 MB, is listed with the reason instead of being guessed at.

## What is on the screen

[Section titled “What is on the screen”](#what-is-on-the-screen)

| Part                   | What it shows or does                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Totals                 | Done, open and the number of plan files of the project, with a bar; the numbers are always written beside it                   |
| **Files and sections** | One row per file with its numbers; open a file to see its headings, and a heading opens the file at that line in the Code view |
| **Open items**         | Every open item with its file, line and heading                                                                                |
| Click an item          | The Code view opens the file at the item’s line                                                                                |
| **Copy**               | The item’s text goes to the clipboard                                                                                          |
| **Hand to an agent**   | The dialog described above                                                                                                     |
| Refresh button         | Reloads at once, next to **Plan paths**                                                                                        |

## Keyboard

[Section titled “Keyboard”](#keyboard)

`Tab` reaches the search, the file list and the items. From the search `↓` goes to the first item; in the list `↑` and `↓` move between items and `Home` and `End` jump to the ends; `Enter` or `Space` opens the item in the Code view. `Esc` in the search clears it; `Esc` in a dialog closes it.

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

The view reloads by itself when a plan file changes on disk, for example after an agent ticked a box. It checks the files’ sizes and modification times every few seconds, and only while the window is visible and focused.

* Keep one checkbox per line of work. An agent that finishes an item ticks it in the file, and the Plan view picks it up without a refresh.
* Plan files written by the [agent-skills](/skills/) workflow (`.docs/TODO.md` and `.docs/plan/`) are found with the default patterns.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Tasks and trackers](/agent/tasks/)Tasks from your tracker, written into TASK.md and started with an agent.

[Editor and files](/agent/code/)The Code view, where an item opens at its line.

[Agents and sessions](/agent/sessions/)The sessions a plan item can be handed to.

[Documents](/agent/documents/)The README, the changelog and the .docs folder, read safely.

# Plugins and Claude Design

> Plugins & MCP in Skribly Agent installs and switches Claude Code plugins, hands a Claude Design package to an agent and manages the Cursor tab.

The **Plugins & MCP** view has five tabs. This page covers three of them: **Claude Plugins** (the Claude Code plugin catalogue), **Claude Design** (from a design to code, with shortcuts to claude.ai) and **Cursor**. The **MCP servers** tab is described in [MCP servers](/agent/mcp/) and **Extensions** in [Extensions](/agent/extensions/).

![The Claude Plugins tab: five installed Claude Code plugins with their scope and switches, and the catalogue with search, categories and Install buttons](/_astro/agent-plugins.DZRwwCjw_Z1zuK5U.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Plugins & MCP** in the activity bar on the left, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Plugins & MCP**.

On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` in place of `⌘`. The view has no number shortcut: `⌘1` to `⌘9` stay with the first nine views. The tabs are the switch at the top right of the view.

## Claude Code plugins

[Section titled “Claude Code plugins”](#claude-code-plugins)

The **Claude Plugins** tab lists the plugins Claude Code has installed and the catalogue you can add from. Skribly runs `claude plugin …`, so Claude Code itself takes care of the file format and locking.

### How to install a plugin

[Section titled “How to install a plugin”](#how-to-install-a-plugin)

1. Choose where it applies in **Install and enable for**.

2. Find the plugin. The catalogue opens on **Recommended**. Use the filters **Design**, **Code and review**, **Documents**, **Integrations** or **All**, or type in the search field, which searches the whole catalogue.

3. Press **Install** on the card. Each card shows where the plugin works: Claude Code, Cowork or claude.ai.

4. Start a new Claude Code session. A change takes effect from the next one.

| Scope in the interface | Settings file                                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **everywhere**         | `~/.claude/settings.json`                               |
| **project (repo)**     | `<project>/.claude/settings.json`, shared with the team |
| **project (only me)**  | `<project>/.claude/settings.local.json`                 |

The two project scopes need a project selected in the top bar.

### How to switch off or remove a plugin

[Section titled “How to switch off or remove a plugin”](#how-to-switch-off-or-remove-a-plugin)

Each row of **Installed** has a switch, its scope as a badge, a button to the plugin’s repository and **Uninstall**. The switch turns the plugin off without removing it. **Uninstall** removes it from that scope.

### What the tab needs

[Section titled “What the tab needs”](#what-the-tab-needs)

A badge shows **Claude Code CLI detected** or **without Claude Code CLI**. Without the CLI the catalogue comes from Claude Code’s local copy, `~/.claude/plugins/plugin-directory-cache-v2.json`, and the switch edits the `enabledPlugins` key of the settings file. Installing and uninstalling need the CLI. The catalogue is cached for ten minutes, and **Refresh** reloads it at once. Listing and installing plugins are network calls, so the **No network calls by the app** switch blocks them; see [Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/).

## Claude Design to code

[Section titled “Claude Design to code”](#claude-design-to-code)

![The Claude Design tab of Plugins & MCP: Open Claude Design, Choose package, the agent that will implement it, and two imported design packages with Implement buttons](/_astro/agent-claude-design.Dym6MRvX_Z2xoHr.webp)

You design in Claude Design, and an agent builds the design in your project with its own components and tokens.

### How to implement a design

[Section titled “How to implement a design”](#how-to-implement-a-design)

1. Open the **Claude Design** tab and select a project in the top bar.

2. Press **Open Claude Design**. A Claude tab opens in the [Browser](/agent/browser/), in its own profile, and you sign in once.

3. In Claude Design export the design as a `.zip` or as standalone HTML. The file is saved in `Skribly Design` in your Downloads folder and appears under **Imported from Claude**.

4. Choose the agent that will build it next to **Will implement**.

5. Press **Implement** next to the package. To use a package that is not on the list press **Choose package…** (`.zip`, `.html`, `.htm` or `.md`; on macOS also a folder).

What happens next:

* The package is extracted to `.skribly/design/<name>-<date>/` in the project. `__MACOSX`, `.DS_Store`, `node_modules` and `.git` are left out, a single folder inside the archive is flattened, and paths that leave the folder are refused. The folder is excluded from git locally.
* Skribly looks for an entry file: `handoff*.md`, `readme*.md`, `claude*.md` or `prompt*.md`, then `index.html`, then any `.html`.
* The agent opens in the Agents view with a prompt. It reviews the package and the existing code, lists a plan and waits for your “ok”. It keeps the colours, typography, spacing, texts and assets, builds from the project’s components instead of copying the HTML, then checks the result in the preview at desktop and phone size and checks accessibility. It commits only after you agree, without `Co-Authored-By` lines.

### Claude in Skribly

[Section titled “Claude in Skribly”](#claude-in-skribly)

At the bottom of the tab are shortcuts to claude.ai. A click opens the page in the Claude tab of the Browser. The button with the arrow, **Open in system browser**, opens it in your browser instead.

| Shortcut                   | Address                       |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| **Claude Design**          | `https://claude.ai/design`    |
| **Artifacts**              | `https://claude.ai/artifacts` |
| **Claude Code on the web** | `https://claude.ai/code`      |
| **Scheduled**              | `https://claude.ai/scheduled` |
| **Customize**              | `https://claude.ai/customize` |

## The Cursor tab

[Section titled “The Cursor tab”](#the-cursor-tab)

The **Cursor** tab shows what is on this computer and edits the project’s Cursor rules.

| Part                             | What it does                                                                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Cursor app**                   | Shows where the app is, or **Download Cursor** when it is not found                                                                                                           |
| The `cursor` command             | Shown when it is in your `PATH`. It is needed to open files and install extensions. In Cursor run the command palette entry `Shell Command: Install 'cursor' command in PATH` |
| `cursor-agent`                   | The Cursor agent in a terminal. **Install cursor-agent** installs it, and when it is there you can sign in and press **Run** to start it in the Agents view                   |
| **Skribly editor**               | **Set Cursor as the editor** makes files from the Code, Audits and Skills views open in Cursor                                                                                |
| **Open the project in Cursor**   | Opens the selected project in the Cursor app. It needs a project                                                                                                              |
| **Cursor MCP servers**           | Goes to the **MCP servers** tab                                                                                                                                               |
| **Cursor themes and extensions** | Goes to the Appearance view                                                                                                                                                   |

### How to write a Cursor rule

[Section titled “How to write a Cursor rule”](#how-to-write-a-cursor-rule)

Cursor rules are files in `.cursor/rules` of the project.

1. Select a project, then press **New rule** under **Project rules**.

2. Fill in the **File name (without .mdc)**, a description, the **File patterns (globs, comma separated)** and the **Rule text (Markdown)**.

3. Tick **Always apply (alwaysApply)** if the rule should always go into the context. Save.

Each rule in the list shows how it applies: **always**, **for files**, **by description** or **manually**. The row has a switch for always applying, and buttons to edit, to open the file in the editor and to delete. The tab reads rules up to three folders deep.

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

Install a plugin for **project (repo)** only when the whole team should have it. Use **project (only me)** to try one first.

* Plugins you add are code from a third party. Read what a plugin does before you switch it on.
* A Claude Design package can be large. The agent works from the extracted folder, so you can delete `.skribly/design/<name>-<date>/` when the work is done.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[MCP servers](/agent/mcp/)The servers of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini.

[Extensions](/agent/extensions/)Your own prompts, rules, skills, servers and commands.

[Browser](/agent/browser/)Where Claude Design opens, in its own profile.

[Skills](/agent/skills/)Skills for each agent from the agent-skills repository.

# Resources

> The Resources view of Skribly Agent shows memory, processor and ports of every pane and its processes next to free memory and swap, and can stop one process.

The **Resources** view shows how much memory and processor every pane of Skribly Agent takes, counting its whole process tree: the agent, its shells, test runners, dev servers and headless browsers. With many agents a laptop can run out of memory, and it is hard to see which agent is the cause. This view puts the panes side by side with the free memory and swap of the machine, and says in words when free memory is short.

![The Resources view: memory of the app panes, free memory and swap, and a table of panes with memory, processor, processes and ports, one pane opened to its largest processes](/_astro/agent-resources.DvQchLHH_Z1j5hem.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Resources** (the gauge) in the activity bar, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Resources**.

On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` wherever this page says `⌘`. The view has no number shortcut. It reads every 3 seconds, and only while it is open and the window is visible. Another view, a minimised window or a window hidden in the tray reads nothing; coming back reads at once. **Refresh** reads now.

## What is on the screen

[Section titled “What is on the screen”](#what-is-on-the-screen)

| Part            | What it shows                                                                                                                       |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **App panes**   | The memory of all panes’ trees together, their processor share and the number of processes                                          |
| **Free memory** | What the system can still give, the total, and a bar of the share in use                                                            |
| **Swap**        | Swap in use and its size (on Windows, the page file)                                                                                |
| Warning         | Appears when free memory is short, see below                                                                                        |
| Table of panes  | One row per pane, largest first: **Memory**, **Processor**, **Processes** and **Ports** (the listening TCP ports of the whole tree) |

A number that the system does not give reads **no data**, never `0`. Windows gives no processor share per process, so that column reads **no data** there.

### The warning

[Section titled “The warning”](#the-warning)

A warning appears above the numbers when free memory is short:

* **Free memory is short.** when less than 12% is free, or less than 1 GB.
* **Memory is almost gone.** when less than 5% is free, or less than 10% with swap more than 80% full.

It names the largest pane and says what to do: stop an unneeded process or close an unused pane.

### How the numbers are counted

[Section titled “How the numbers are counted”](#how-the-numbers-are-counted)

| Number      | macOS                                  | Linux                                   | Windows                      |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Processes   | `ps`                                   | `ps`                                    | `Win32_Process` (PowerShell) |
| Memory      | Resident memory (RSS)                  | Resident memory (RSS)                   | Working set                  |
| Processor   | Recent average share of one core       | Average share since the process started | Not given                    |
| Ports       | `lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` for the tree | `ss -ltnp`                              | `netstat -ano`               |
| Free memory | Free, inactive and speculative pages   | `MemAvailable`                          | Free physical memory         |

A pane’s tree is the pane’s own process and every process whose parent chain leads to it. Memory shared between processes counts with each of them, so a tree’s total can be higher than what it really holds. A processor share above 100% means more than one core.

## How to see what a pane runs

[Section titled “How to see what a pane runs”](#how-to-see-what-a-pane-runs)

1. Click a row of the table, or press `Enter` or `Space` on it.

2. Read **The pane’s largest processes**, up to eight: process id, memory, processor, ports and the command line. A note says how many processes the tree has in all.

3. Press **Go** on the row to open the pane in the [Agents view](/agent/terminals/). The button is off for helper panes, such as the terminal of the Code view, which have no place there.

## How to stop a process

[Section titled “How to stop a process”](#how-to-stop-a-process)

1. Open the pane and find the process, for example a runaway test runner or a forgotten dev server.

2. Press **Stop…** on its line. The dialog **Stop this process?** names the command, the process id, the pane and its memory.

3. Press **Stop process N**.

The pane’s own process has no **Stop…** button, only the note **pane process**: close the pane instead. **Copy process line** puts the process id, memory, processor, ports and the command into the clipboard.

What stopping does and does not do:

* It acts only on the process id you chose, never on a name or a pattern.
* Right before it acts, the app reads the process table again. It refuses when the process id is no longer in that pane’s tree, now runs a different command, is the pane’s own process, or is the app itself.
* On macOS and Linux it sends `SIGTERM`, so the program can end cleanly. On Windows the process ends at once.
* The pane and the rest of its tree keep running.

## Keyboard

[Section titled “Keyboard”](#keyboard)

| Key                   | Action                                                    |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `↑` `↓`, `Home` `End` | Move between panes                                        |
| `Enter`, `Space`      | Open or close the processes of a pane                     |
| `Tab`                 | Move through the actions of the open pane                 |
| `Esc`                 | Close the open pane and return to its row; close a dialog |

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

Look at the **Ports** column when a dev server will not start: a forgotten process of another pane may hold the port.

* The view uses only the tools of your operating system on your machine. It makes no network call and writes nothing.
* Run fewer agents at once when the warning appears, or stop the dev servers and test runners that you no longer need.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Terminals and sessions](/agent/terminals/)The panes this view measures.

[Worktrees](/agent/worktrees/)See which worktrees still have a pane working in them.

[Troubleshooting](/agent/troubleshooting/)Common problems and their fixes.

# Review notes

> Note a line or a range of a diff in Skribly Agent, keep the notes in one list, and send them all to an agent as one message that you read first.

When you read a diff, you can write a note on a line or on a range of lines, and send all the notes to an agent as one message. The agent gets the file, the lines, the quoted code and your text for every note, so it can work through them without the diff. Nothing is sent before you press **Send**, and the message is shown whole before it goes.

![A diff with two review notes listed below it, each with its file and lines, and the button Send to the agent](/_astro/agent-code-review.Ucb9j_vO_Z1GXgRD.webp)

On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` wherever this page says `⌘` or `⌥`.

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

Review notes live in the diff of the **Code & git** view.

* Open **Code & git** (`⌘4`), stay on the **Changes and commit** tab, and click a file. Its diff opens next to the list.
* The bar above the diff has the **Add a note** button and the number of notes.

The notes list appears under the diff as soon as there is a note.

## How to write a note

[Section titled “How to write a note”](#how-to-write-a-note)

1. In the diff, select a line or a range of lines. Without a selection, the line of the cursor is used.

2. Press `⌘⌥M`, or press **Add a note** above the diff, or right-click and choose **Note on the diff…**.

3. Type what the agent should change in these lines.

4. Press `⌘↩` or **Save the note** to keep it. `Esc` or **Cancel** drops it and returns the focus to the diff.

A note in the right column is about the new lines. A note in the left column is about the old version, and is marked **old version**. A deleted file takes notes on its old lines, marked **deleted file, old lines**. A binary file shows no lines: it takes one note on the whole file, and the button there is **Note on the file**.

Lines with a note carry a mark in the margin of the diff. Hover the mark to read the note.

## How to manage the notes

[Section titled “How to manage the notes”](#how-to-manage-the-notes)

The list under the diff, **Review notes (N)**, holds every note of the project, not only those of the open file. It is sorted the way the agent will read it: by file, then by line.

| Button                    | What it does                                                     |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Arrow, **Go to the line** | Opens the file and puts the cursor on the first line of the note |
| Pencil, **Edit**          | Opens the note in the form to change its text                    |
| Bin, **Delete**           | Removes the note                                                 |
| **Discard all**           | Removes every note, after a question: **Discard all the notes?** |
| **Send to the agent…**    | Opens the dialog described below                                 |

## How to send the notes to an agent

[Section titled “How to send the notes to an agent”](#how-to-send-the-notes-to-an-agent)

1. Press **Send to the agent…** over the list. The dialog **Send the notes to the agent** opens.

2. Read the message in the field. It is read-only and it is exactly what goes to the agent.

3. Pick a session under **To**. Sessions of this project come first, and the session that runs in the project’s folder is chosen for you.

4. Press **Send** (`⌘↩`). The message goes into the terminal of the session, as every other text sent to an agent does, and the notes that were in it are removed.

![The dialog Send the notes to the agent: the full message with both notes and quoted code, and the list of sessions it can go to](/_astro/agent-code-review-send.BrL4hAdU_5pToF.webp)

The message starts with the number of notes and files and a short instruction: go through the notes in order, change only what a note asks for, and report what was done for each note by its number. Then comes one block per note: a heading with the file name and the line range, the quoted lines in a fenced block, and your text. The file name and the quoted lines are written so that spaces, backticks and control characters cannot break the layout.

The dialog lists only running sessions. If there is none, it says so: start an agent in the Agents view and come back, because the notes stay saved.

## Limits

[Section titled “Limits”](#limits)

| Limit                 | Value            |
| --------------------- | ---------------- |
| Notes at once         | 200              |
| Text of a note        | 4,000 characters |
| Quoted code of a note | 4,000 characters |

Notes are stored in the app’s data folder, per project, until you send or discard them, so they survive a restart. A project that is a session’s worktree has its own list.

## Tips

[Section titled “Tips”](#tips)

Tip

Write each note as an instruction to change something (“Rename this to `total`”, “Add a check for an empty cart”), not as a question. The message tells the agent to change only what a note asks for.

* Notes on staged and on working diffs go into the same list and the same message.
* You can write notes, close the app and send them tomorrow.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Changes and commits](/agent/changes/)Where the diffs come from: the index, discard and commit.

[Editor and files](/agent/code/)Send selected code to an agent instead of notes on a diff.

[Terminals and sessions](/agent/terminals/)The sessions a message can be sent to.

# Session history

> The session history of Skribly Agent lists past sessions of Claude Code, Codex and Copilot CLI, filters them and resumes one in its own folder.

The session history is one list of the past sessions of the agents whose own session files Skribly can read: Claude Code, Codex and Copilot CLI. For the open project or for all projects it shows the agent, the folder, the branch, when the session started and ended, the first line of what it was about and the tokens it used. Choosing a session reopens it in its folder with that agent’s own resume command.

![The Session history dialog: search, agent filter, This project and All projects, and five past sessions of Claude Code, Codex and Copilot CLI with Resume](/_astro/agent-session-history.DQLvDzrj_Z1k7WJ2.webp)

## Open the dialog

[Section titled “Open the dialog”](#open-the-dialog)

* Press **History** in the toolbar of the Agents view, or
* press `Ctrl+B`, then `h`, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Agent session history and resume**.

The list is read when the dialog opens and when you press **Refresh**. There is no timer, so a closed dialog or a hidden app never reads a file.

## How to find and resume a session

[Section titled “How to find and resume a session”](#how-to-find-and-resume-a-session)

1. Open the dialog. The search box has the focus.

2. Type in **Search the first line, folder, branch or agent…**. The search looks in the first line, the folder, the branch, the project name, the agent name and the session id, and every word has to match.

3. Narrow the list with the agent filter, which offers the agents that have sessions, and with **Scope**: **This project** or **All projects**.

4. Choose a session, or move to it with `↑` and `↓` and press `Enter`. A new pane opens in the session’s folder and runs the agent’s resume command.

The list is newest first. It holds the sessions of the last 90 days, at most 500, and says when it was cut.

## What resuming runs

[Section titled “What resuming runs”](#what-resuming-runs)

| Agent       | Command run in the session’s folder |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Claude Code | `claude --resume <id>`              |
| Codex       | `codex resume <id>`                 |
| Copilot CLI | `copilot --resume=<id>`             |

* A session whose folder no longer exists is greyed out and says so. Nothing is started.
* A session of an agent without a resume command opens a new session of that agent in the folder instead. Today all three listed agents have one.
* The command is built from fixed parts and the session id. An id has to be a canonical UUID, the agent has to be one of the three and the session has to be in the list the app just read. Nothing else from a session file reaches a command line.

## What the app reads

[Section titled “What the app reads”](#what-the-app-reads)

Skribly only reads these files and never writes into them.

| Agent       | Files                                                           |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Claude Code | `<CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR or ~/.claude>/projects/<folder>/<id>.jsonl` |
| Codex       | `<CODEX_HOME or ~/.codex>/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*.jsonl`  |
| Copilot CLI | `<COPILOT_HOME or ~/.copilot>/session-state/<id>/events.jsonl`  |

* Only the first 256 KB of each file is read, so a huge session costs the same as a small one. From it the app takes the id, the start time, the folder, the branch and the first line of the first message you wrote.
* The end time is the time the file was last changed.
* The first line is cut to one plain line of 140 characters. It is shown only in this dialog; it is not logged, not sent anywhere and not part of any command.
* Tokens come from the same reader as the [usage board](/agent/usage/) and cover the last 14 days. An older session, or one whose files carry no token numbers, shows none, not a zero.
* Files that are broken, empty or not in the layout above are skipped.

## Keyboard

[Section titled “Keyboard”](#keyboard)

`↑` and `↓` move through the list, `Ctrl+Home` and `Ctrl+End` jump to its ends, `Enter` resumes the marked session and `Esc` closes the dialog. The filters are ordinary controls in the tab order.

Tip

Shortcuts on this site use `⌘`. On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` instead. The `Ctrl+B` prefix is the same on every system.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Agents and sessions](/agent/sessions/)Resume after restart, which brings back the open panes.

[Token use and resources](/agent/usage/)Where the token numbers of a session come from.

[Data and network](/agent/data-and-network/)What the app reads and where it connects.

# Agents and sessions

> Start a session in Skribly Agent, read the agent states and Why this state, use the agent panel, toolbar and chat mode, resume after a restart and hand work over.

A session is one agent running in one pane: a terminal with the agent, or a chat. You start it from **New session**, and the app detects what the agent is doing, tells you when it needs you and brings it back after a restart.

![The agent panel open on the right of the Agents view: a Claude Code chat with its message field, model, Edit and Remote controls](/_astro/agent-panel.BNBM_C3e_heU9k.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Agents** in the activity bar, or press `⌘2`, or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Agents**, or **New session: …** for an agent.

Shortcuts on this site use `⌘`. On Windows and Linux use `Ctrl` instead. The `Ctrl+B` prefix is the same on every system.

## How to start a session

[Section titled “How to start a session”](#how-to-start-a-session)

1. Press **New session** on the tab bar, or `Ctrl+B a`, or a split button in a pane header.

2. Pick an agent card, or **Terminal** for a plain shell. An agent that is not installed is dimmed and shows **Install …** and the install command.

3. Choose the **Project** and the **Working copy**: the main one, an existing worktree or **+ New worktree…** with a branch, which is created from the project’s base branch. Choose the **Machine**: **This computer** or an SSH machine.

4. Optionally fill **Name for the CLI and other agents**, such as `reviewer` (lower case letters, digits, `_` and `-`, up to 32 characters), choose the **Mode**, **Terminal** or **Chat**, and write the **First message (optional)**. In chat mode, tick **can modify files** if the agent may edit.

5. Press **Run**, or `Enter` in the message field (`Shift+Enter` adds a line).

In terminal mode the app opens a login shell (`$SHELL -l`, `pwsh` or `powershell.exe` on Windows) and types the agent’s command into it, with the first message as an argument where the agent accepts one. An agent that does not, such as OpenCode or Aider, gets it typed in after it starts. The session has the variable `SKRIBLY_TERMINAL=<id>`.

## Agent states

[Section titled “Agent states”](#agent-states)

The state of a session is read from the agent’s screen and its output. No plugin or hook in the agent is needed.

| State                      | What it means                                                    |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **starting**               | The session has just been created                                |
| **working**                | The agent is working: there is activity in the output            |
| **waiting for a decision** | The agent asks for approval or a choice and waits for you        |
| **done**                   | The agent finished its turn and you have not seen the result yet |
| **ready**                  | You saw the result; the agent waits for the next prompt          |
| **finished**               | The process has exited; the details have the exit code           |

* **The agent’s screen.** Each agent has rules for the waiting and working states, for example the “Do you want to…?” question of Claude Code or the approval dialog of Codex. General rules catch `(y/n)`, “Press Enter to continue” and a password prompt. The rules are careful: a false wait is worse than a late one.
* **Output activity.** With no matching rule, output within the last 1.5 seconds means working. After 2.5 seconds of silence the turn ends: done if there was real work and you have not seen it, otherwise ready.
* **Agent recognition.** The app checks the foreground process, so a Terminal pane where you started `codex` by hand gets Codex’s avatar and rules.
* **Viewing.** A done pane that is visible in the focused window becomes ready.
* **Process exit.** The session becomes finished.

### Why this state?

[Section titled “Why this state?”](#why-this-state)

Press the state badge in the pane header. The dialog shows the state, the recognised agent, the source of the state (agent screen pattern, output activity, process exited or none), the foreground process, the rule that matched and the last 24 lines of the screen. Look there first when a state seems wrong.

## The agent panel

[Section titled “The agent panel”](#the-agent-panel)

The panel on the right opens over any view with the button next to the search box or `⌘⇧A`. Each project keeps its own conversations, and they come back after a restart. Drag the left edge to change the width. **New conversation** starts another one and **Close the panel** hides it.

| Tool                   | What it does                                                                                      |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Agent menu             | Chooses the agent, or installs one that is missing. Changing the agent starts a new conversation  |
| **Change model**       | The default model, the agent’s list or any name you type; the refresh button asks the agent again |
| **Effort**             | Claude Code only: `--effort` from low to max                                                      |
| **Slash commands**     | Commands from the agent, the project, your home folder and plugins. `/clear` starts over          |
| **Plugins**            | Turns Claude Code plugins on and off; the next message uses the change                            |
| **Attach files**       | Attaches files. You can also drop files on the box or paste an image                              |
| **Edit** or **Plan**   | Whether the agent may change files                                                                |
| **Remote**             | Starts a Claude Code session with Remote Control, to control it from your phone or claude.ai/code |
| **Open in a terminal** | Continues the same conversation in a terminal                                                     |

Under the message box you see the session time, the subagents and the context, as far as the agent reports them.

## The toolbar under a pane

[Section titled “The toolbar under a pane”](#the-toolbar-under-a-pane)

An agent pane has the same tools in a bar under it: **Slash commands**, **Change model**, **Effort**, **Plugins**, **Reload plugins**, **Attach files** and **Remote**. They type into the session, so `/model`, `/effort`, `/reload-plugins` and `/remote-control` behave as if you typed them. The bar holds back while the agent is asking a question, because text sent then would answer it. Subagents and context in a terminal come from the Claude Code transcript, so other agents show only the time.

## Chat mode

[Section titled “Chat mode”](#chat-mode)

A chat is an agent run without an interface: each message is a separate run that carries the session id of the last reply, so the agent remembers the conversation and no process runs between messages. The pane shows text, tool calls and errors.

| Key           | Action              |
| ------------- | ------------------- |
| `Enter`       | Send                |
| `Shift+Enter` | New line            |
| **Stop**      | Interrupt the reply |

Chats are kept in the interface’s memory and do not come back after a restart; continue the conversation in a terminal with **Open in a terminal**. Kimi CLI has no chat mode. The agents and their flags are on [Supported agents](/agent/agents/).

## Resume after restart

[Section titled “Resume after restart”](#resume-after-restart)

**Settings → Sessions & control → Restore sessions after restart** is on by default.

* Tabs, splits and panes return to their places with the same ids, names, worktrees and tasks.
* An agent for which the app found a native session id continues the conversation and gets a **resumed** badge. Claude Code, Cursor Agent, Droid and Qwen Code use `--resume <id>`, Codex uses `codex resume <id>`, Copilot CLI `--resume=<id>`, OpenCode, Crush and Kimi CLI `--session <id>` and Goose `goose session --resume --session-id <id>`. A custom agent uses the resume arguments of its definition.
* Other panes, which are shells, agents without a session, Amp, Gemini CLI, Aider and SSH sessions, start as a fresh shell in the same folder with a hint of the command that starts the agent again.

Quitting the app ends all terminal processes; there is no background server. Continuity comes from the agents’ native resume and from state files. Panes of earlier sessions, not only the ones open at the last quit, are in the [session history](/agent/session-history/).

## Broadcast

[Section titled “Broadcast”](#broadcast)

Send one prompt to several agents. Tick the checkbox in the pane headers, type in the field on the tab bar (**Select panels (☑) to send them the same thing**, which reads **To N selected…** once you tick some) and press `Enter` or **Send to the checked panes**. The text is delivered to every running pane as if you pasted it and confirmed it with `Enter`. Exited panes are skipped.

## Handing off work

[Section titled “Handing off work”](#handing-off-work)

The hand-off button in a pane header passes the work to another agent without replaying the conversation.

1. Press **Send request**. The current agent saves its state, what is done, the next step, decisions and open questions, in a file: `.skribly/tasks/<KEY>/STATE.md` when the session is about a task, otherwise `.skribly/handoff.md`.

2. Press **Run** and the new agent’s name. It starts in the same folder and worktree, next to the previous one, with the prompt to read the state file, run `git status` and `git diff`, summarise in three points and continue.

Do step 2 after step 1. The new agent then starts from a few dozen lines of state instead of the whole transcript.

## The agent overview

[Section titled “The agent overview”](#the-agent-overview)

Press the grid button on the tab bar or `Ctrl+B o` for the **Agent overview**: a grid of live previews of all sessions, with the ones that need you first. Previews are read only while the overview is on screen.

## Related pages

[Section titled “Related pages”](#related-pages)

[Attention inbox](/agent/inbox/)The sessions that wait for you, and the notifications.

[Supported agents](/agent/agents/)The 13 agents and what each supports.

[Terminals](/agent/terminals/)Shell panes, SSH machines and the Code view terminal.

[Workspaces](/agent/workspaces/)Tabs, splits and the workspace sidebar.

# Settings

> Every section of Settings in Skribly Agent, option by option with its default, from appearance and trackers to sessions, cost, the command guard, Docker and updates.

**Settings** holds everything you can change in Skribly Agent. It has sixteen sections in a list on the left. Settings are saved on this device in the data directory; tokens are encrypted with the system keychain. Nothing is sent anywhere when you change a setting.

![Settings, Appearance and tour, in the night theme: the list of sections on the left, and on the right the theme mode, the text size at 13 px, the interface language, the day and night themes and the app tour](/_astro/agent-settings.D_OQtHEz_ZEt1WI.webp)

## Open the view

[Section titled “Open the view”](#open-the-view)

* Click **Settings** at the bottom of the activity bar on the left (the gear), or
* open the command palette (`⌘K`) and choose **Settings**.

The view remembers the section you used last. Some buttons elsewhere in the app open a section directly. `⌘` is `Ctrl` on Windows and Linux.

## The sections

[Section titled “The sections”](#the-sections)

| Section                    | What it controls                                                                                | Details                                               |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| **Appearance and tour**    | Theme mode, text size, interface language, themes, the app tour                                 | [Below](#appearance-and-tour)                         |

| **Privacy and network**    | Every connection, folder and port of the app, and the switch that turns the network off         | [Data, privacy and network](/agent/data-and-network/) |
