# Agent tooling

> Commands of the agent-skills CLI that make coding agents safer and cheaper - a delete guard, a status line, read-only permission presets, an MCP smoke test and a coding agent job for CI.

In development

The commands on this page ship in the next release; the released agent-skills 0.3.0 does not have them yet.

These commands sit next to the skills without being skills. Each is Node with no dependencies, runs on macOS, Linux and Windows, and every one that writes takes `--dry-run`.

| Command                                    | What it does                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `agent-skills hooks install --agent-guard` | a delete guard hook for every agent that has hooks                                                                |
| `agent-skills guard "<command>"`           | says whether the guard would stop a command                                                                       |
| `agent-skills statusline [install]`        | one short status line: agent, model, branch, task, session tokens                                                 |
| `agent-skills permissions [--dry-run]`     | allow lists of read-only commands per agent, from `.skribly/project.json`                                         |
| `agent-skills mcp-smoke`                   | starts each configured MCP server, lists its tools, calls one read-only tool                                      |
| `templates/ci/`                            | a coding agent in CI on an issue label: plan, code, review, draft pull request                                    |
| `agent-skills init --mcp`                  | adds the official MCP server of each detected framework to each agent’s project MCP file                          |
| `agent-skills rules [--check]`             | the rule dictionary for the files in hand, and its line checks over a project ([Rule dictionary](/skills/rules/)) |
| `templates/nightly/`                       | a nightly report of a repository: checks, audit, outdated packages, agent branches                                |
| `deps-update/scripts/dependabot.mjs`       | one Dependabot preset for the detected stack                                                                      |
| `/upgrade`                                 | a major version of a framework or runtime by its migration guide, one area at a time                              |

## Delete guard

[Section titled “Delete guard”](#delete-guard)

```bash
agent-skills hooks install --agent-guard                 # Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode
agent-skills hooks install --agent-guard --agents all    # also Cursor and GitHub Copilot
agent-skills hooks status --agent-guard
agent-skills hooks uninstall --agent-guard
```

The guard reads each shell command an agent is about to run. These make the agent **ask you** instead of running it:

* a recursive or forced delete of the file system root, the home folder or a folder above it, a `.git` folder, anything outside the project or the whole project;
* a delete of 20 or more tracked files at once;
* `git clean --force`, and `rsync --delete` into those places;
* a delete hidden in inline code (`node -e`, `python -c`, `sh -c`, `eval`, PowerShell `-Command`).

Deleting a few files inside the project, or ignored folders such as `node_modules` and `dist`, passes. The guard fails closed: an option it does not know counts as recursive and forced, wrappers such as `sudo`, `env` and `xargs` are looked through, and a path it cannot resolve asks. Install and uninstall touch only the guard’s own entries; your own hooks stay.

| Agent          | File                                             | Answer                                         |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Claude Code    | `.claude/settings.json`                          | asks you                                       |
| Codex          | `.codex/hooks.json`                              | refuses with the reason, so the agent asks you |
| Gemini CLI     | `.gemini/settings.json`                          | refuses with the reason, so the agent asks you |
| OpenCode       | `.opencode/plugins/agent-skills-delete-guard.js` | refuses with the reason                        |
| Cursor         | `.cursor/hooks.json`                             | asks you                                       |
| GitHub Copilot | `.github/hooks/agent-skills-delete-guard.json`   | refuses with the reason                        |

The guard itself lives in `.agents/hooks/delete-guard.mjs`: commit that folder with the hook files, or run the install once per person. Codex runs hooks only with `codex_hooks = true` under `[features]` in `~/.codex/config.toml`.

## Status line

[Section titled “Status line”](#status-line)

```bash
agent-skills statusline install            # Claude Code: statusLine in ~/.claude/settings.json
agent-skills statusline --agent codex      # in tmux or a shell prompt
```

One line such as `claude · Model X · feat/cart · task 482 · 42k tok (21%)`: the agent, the model, the git branch, the task of `.tasks/` whose `STATE.md` names that branch, and the tokens of the session. Codex and Gemini CLI have no status line of their own, so for them the line goes into tmux (`status-right "#(agent-skills statusline --agent codex --no-stdin)"`) or a prompt. A `statusLine` that is not ours is kept unless you pass `--force`.

## Permission presets

[Section titled “Permission presets”](#permission-presets)

```bash
agent-skills permissions --dry-run
agent-skills permissions --agents claude,codex
```

Writes allow lists of read-only commands so agents ask less: `git status`, `git diff`, `git log`, `grep`, plus the `test`, `lint` and `typecheck` commands of the profile when each is a plain command. A command with shell operators, quotes or variables, or with a word that writes, pushes, deletes, installs or reaches the network (`--fix`, `--write`, `push`, `rm`, `curl`, `npx`), is listed as `skipped` and never allowed.

| Agent       | File                                         |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Claude Code | `.claude/settings.json`, `permissions.allow` |
| Codex       | `.codex/rules/agent-skills.rules`            |
| Gemini CLI  | `.gemini/settings.json`, `tools.allowed`     |
| OpenCode    | `opencode.json`, `permission.bash`           |

Entries are added; your own allow and deny entries stay. Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode match by prefix, so keep write flags out of the profile’s commands. Cursor, Copilot and Devin keep their allow lists in their own settings, which this command does not write.

## MCP smoke test

[Section titled “MCP smoke test”](#mcp-smoke-test)

```bash
agent-skills mcp-smoke --dry-run          # what would be started
agent-skills mcp-smoke --timeout 15
agent-skills mcp-smoke --server notes --no-call
```

Reads the MCP servers of `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.gemini/settings.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json`, `opencode.json` and `.codex/config.toml`. Each local server is started without a shell, asked for its tools, and when a tool says it is read-only and needs no arguments, that tool is called; then the server is stopped. Remote servers are listed as skipped and never contacted. One line per server (`ok`, `fail`, `skip`), and exit code 1 when one fails. In a repository you did not write, run `--dry-run` first: the command starts the programs the project configures.

## A coding agent in CI

[Section titled “A coding agent in CI”](#a-coding-agent-in-ci)

`templates/ci/` in the repository holds a GitHub Actions workflow, a GitLab CI file and `run-agent.mjs`. Adding a label to an issue runs the agent in three phases, plan, code and review, with a budget of turns, minutes and changed files, and ends with a draft pull or merge request. Nothing merges. Secrets come only from the CI secret store, and the issue text never reaches a shell line. The same runner works from a timer on your own server.

## Framework MCP servers

[Section titled “Framework MCP servers”](#framework-mcp-servers)

```bash
agent-skills init                 # names the official MCP servers it found
agent-skills init --mcp --dry-run # what would be added
agent-skills init --mcp
```

`init` offers the MCP server that the vendor of each detected framework publishes: Next.js (`next-devtools-mcp`), the Angular CLI, Svelte, Nuxt (remote), Laravel Boost once `laravel/boost` is installed, Dart and Flutter, Go’s `gopls` and Terraform. Each command is the one on the vendor’s MCP page. `--mcp` adds them to the project MCP file of each chosen agent, in the shape that agent reads: `.mcp.json` (Claude Code), `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json` (Copilot), `.gemini/settings.json` (Gemini CLI and Antigravity) and `.codex/config.toml`. A server you already configured under the same name is never changed, a JSON file keeps a `.bak-agent-skills` copy, and a second run changes nothing. Check the result with `agent-skills mcp-smoke`.

## Nightly report

[Section titled “Nightly report”](#nightly-report)

`templates/nightly/` holds `nightly-report.mjs` (Node with no dependencies) with a systemd user service and timer, and a README with a cron line instead. Each night it runs the checks of `.skribly/nightly.json`, or the plain `test`, `lint`, `typecheck` and `build` commands of `.skribly/project.json`, then `npm audit` or `composer audit` and `npm outdated`, and counts the agent branches and CI agent reports of the last day. It writes `.skribly/reports/nightly-<date>.md` with one line per item: its state, its time and the first error line. Every program starts without a shell and with a timeout; nothing in the repository is installed, fixed, committed or pushed, and nothing is sent anywhere. `--strict` exits 1 on a failure, for a notifier of your own.

## Dependabot preset

[Section titled “Dependabot preset”](#dependabot-preset)

```bash
node skills/deps-update/scripts/dependabot.mjs            # print it
node skills/deps-update/scripts/dependabot.mjs --write    # write .github/dependabot.yml
```

The script reads the stack of the repository and writes one entry per ecosystem and folder (npm, bun, composer, pip, uv, bundler, gomod, cargo, maven, gradle, nuget, docker, docker-compose, terraform and GitHub Actions; test fixtures left out). All entries run weekly on the same day and time (`--day`, `--time`, `--timezone`); minor and patch updates are grouped into one pull request per ecosystem, a major comes alone, and security updates are grouped apart so they arrive at once. An existing different file is kept unless you pass `--force`. The `deps-update` skill offers it and writes it only after your OK.

## Major upgrades

[Section titled “Major upgrades”](#major-upgrades)

`/upgrade` (or `$upgrade` in Codex) moves a project to a new major version of its framework or runtime, such as Next.js 16, Laravel 12 or Django 5. It reads the installed version from the lock file and the migration guide of the target version, and runs the vendor’s own tool (`next upgrade`, `ng update`, a codemod, `rector`, `django-upgrade`, `rails app:update`) only after it shows you that tool’s plan. The guide is split into areas of one commit each. Every area gets a failing or pinning test first, a bump through the package manager, only the changes the guide names and the checks, and waits for your OK before the next one. An area that stays red is reverted alone. Routine minor and patch bumps stay with `deps-update`.

## Read next

[Section titled “Read next”](#read-next)

* [Rule dictionary](/skills/rules/): `agent-skills rules` and `rules --check`.
* [How it works](/skills/how-it-works/): the pipeline and its guardrails.
* [Commits without AI trailers](/skills/commits/): the commit-msg hook and the attribution setting.
* [Troubleshooting](/skills/troubleshooting/): `agent-skills doctor`.

# Trackers

> Connect agent-skills to Redmine, Jira, GitHub, GitLab, Linear or Skribly Tracker, and use the tasks commands that the task skill runs.

The `task` skill fetches issues with a script (`agent-skills tasks`), so the model spends no tokens on HTTP, pagination or re-reading. The first fetch writes `.tasks/<id>/TASK.md`; later fetches print only what changed: new comments, status, a changed description, new attachments.

## Credentials

[Section titled “Credentials”](#credentials)

Put them in environment variables or in `~/.config/agent-skills/credentials.env` (Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.config\agent-skills\credentials.env`). Environment variables win over the file. Start from the template in the repository:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/agent-skills
cp templates/credentials.env.example ~/.config/agent-skills/credentials.env
chmod 600 ~/.config/agent-skills/credentials.env     # doctor warns if others can read it
agent-skills tasks check                             # who am I, per configured tracker
```

Never put tokens in a repository, in `.tasks/` or in a chat. Point at another file with `AGENT_SKILLS_CREDENTIALS`. Inside [Skribly Agent](/agent/tasks/), sessions receive these variables from the app, so no file is needed.

## Skribly Tracker

[Section titled “Skribly Tracker”](#skribly-tracker)

```bash
SKRIBLY_TRACKER_URL=http://localhost:8100   # base URL of the instance
SKRIBLY_TRACKER_TOKEN=...                   # Profile -> API tokens
```

Ids: `ABC-12` or an `/issues/ABC-12` URL on the `SKRIBLY_TRACKER_URL` host. The client uses [REST API v1](/tracker/rest-api/); descriptions and comments are already Markdown, and attachments are downloaded with the same token. “My open tasks” is `assignee=me&status=open&sort=-updated`.

## Redmine

[Section titled “Redmine”](#redmine)

```bash
REDMINE_URL=https://redmine.example.com
REDMINE_API_KEY=...        # My account -> API access key (an admin must enable the REST API)
```

Ids: `123`, `#123` or an `/issues/123` URL. Comments are journal notes.

## Jira Cloud

[Section titled “Jira Cloud”](#jira-cloud)

```bash
JIRA_URL=https://your-team.atlassian.net
JIRA_EMAIL=you@example.com
JIRA_API_TOKEN=...         # id.atlassian.com -> Security -> API tokens
```

## Jira Server / Data Center

[Section titled “Jira Server / Data Center”](#jira-server--data-center)

```bash
JIRA_URL=https://jira.example.com
JIRA_PAT=...               # Profile -> Personal Access Tokens
```

Ids: `ABC-123` or a `/browse/ABC-123` URL. Wiki markup is converted to Markdown.

## GitHub

[Section titled “GitHub”](#github)

```bash
GITHUB_TOKEN=...           # fine-grained token: Issues read (write only to post comments)
GITHUB_API_URL=https://github.example.com/api/v3   # GitHub Enterprise Server only
```

Without a token, a signed-in GitHub CLI (`gh auth login`) is used, and public issues work anonymously at 60 requests an hour. Ids: `7` (the repository of the `origin` remote), `owner/repo#7` or an issue URL.

## GitLab

[Section titled “GitLab”](#gitlab)

```bash
GITLAB_TOKEN=...           # read_api (api to post comments)
GITLAB_URL=https://gitlab.example.com   # default https://gitlab.com
```

Ids: `7`, `group/sub/project#7` or a `/-/issues/7` URL. System notes are skipped.

## Linear

[Section titled “Linear”](#linear)

```bash
LINEAR_API_KEY=lin_api_...  # Settings -> Security & access -> Personal API keys
```

Ids: `ENG-12` or a `linear.app/.../issue/ENG-12/...` URL.

## Which tracker does an id mean?

[Section titled “Which tracker does an id mean?”](#which-tracker-does-an-id-mean)

In order: `--tracker`, the `Tracker:` line in `.tasks/workflow.md`, `AGENT_SKILLS_TRACKER`, then whichever tracker is configured. A configured Redmine wins for plain numbers; GitHub or GitLab when the `origin` remote points there. `ABC-12` can be Jira, Linear or Skribly Tracker: the same three settings decide, otherwise the only configured one is used, and with several you are asked. A task fetched once remembers its tracker.

## Commands

[Section titled “Commands”](#commands)

```bash
agent-skills tasks fetch 123                 # TASK.md; on re-fetch only the changes
agent-skills tasks attachments 123 [name]    # images by default, --all for every file
agent-skills tasks list                      # my open issues in every configured tracker (--json)
agent-skills tasks list --local              # tasks in .tasks/ with status, branch and next step
agent-skills tasks comment-draft 123         # create or show .tasks/123/COMMENT.md
agent-skills tasks comment-draft 123 --post --yes    # publish, only after your explicit OK
agent-skills tasks detect                    # git facts used to write .tasks/workflow.md
agent-skills tasks check                     # configuration and token test
```

## Safety

[Section titled “Safety”](#safety)

* Read-only by default. Writing needs `--post --yes`, and the same text is never posted twice.
* Tokens are sent only to the tracker’s own host. Redirects to another host, such as a CDN serving an attachment, are followed without credentials.
* Behind a corporate proxy with TLS errors, point `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` at the proxy’s CA certificate.

# Train the skills for your project

> Fit agent-skills to one project step by step - agent-skills init, the train-skills loop, switching skills on and off, lessons with a scope and small project skills of your own.

In development

`agent-skills init`, `project enable` and `disable`, `train-skills` and lessons with a scope ship in the next release. In the released agent-skills 0.3.0, install in project scope as on [Install](/skills/install/#user-scope-or-project-scope) and run the `project` skill.

Training the skills means fitting them to one repository: the right skills for its stack, a checked profile of its commands, and the first lessons the agent proved in it. It takes one command and one conversation, and every step that writes waits for your OK.

## 1. Preview the setup

[Section titled “1. Preview the setup”](#1-preview-the-setup)

In the project folder:

```bash
agent-skills init --dry-run
```

It prints what it would do and writes nothing: the stack and commands it found, the skills that fit the stack, the agents it found and the files it would write. Use `--agents claude,codex` (or `--agents all`) when it picks the wrong agents.

## 2. Run init

[Section titled “2. Run init”](#2-run-init)

```bash
agent-skills init
```

It does four things and ends with a short summary:

1. Detects the stack, the commands and the conventions into `.skribly/project.json`. Values you set by hand are kept.
2. Installs, in project scope, only the skills that fit the stack, for every agent you use (one copy per agent).
3. Writes `.tasks/plans/README.md` and `.tasks/specs/README.md`, the conventions of the planning folders.
4. Prints what it found and installed.

A second run changes nothing. Run it again after the stack changes. To undo all of it: `agent-skills uninstall --target all --project .`.

## 3. Ask your agent to train the skills

[Section titled “3. Ask your agent to train the skills”](#3-ask-your-agent-to-train-the-skills)

Open the agent in the project and ask for `/train-skills` (`$train-skills` in Codex). The [`train-skills`](/skills/skill/train-skills/) skill finishes the loop:

1. **Reads the profile** with `AGENTS.md` and the README, and asks you once to confirm the commands and the base branch. Your answer is written into the profile by hand, so it wins over later detection.
2. **Runs the checks once**: install (only with your OK), then lint, typecheck and test, the long ones after asking. For each it notes passed, failed with the first real error line, or missing. It does not fix the project’s code here: a failing check is a finding.
3. **Proposes lessons** for the facts it proved, each with a scope and a source, a `file:line` or a commit. At most five, each saved only on your yes.
4. **Proposes project skills** when the project repeats a procedure no installed skill covers.
5. **Reports** in five lines: what init installed, the profile corrections, each check, the lessons saved, the project skills written or proposed.

## 4. Switch skills on and off

[Section titled “4. Switch skills on and off”](#4-switch-skills-on-and-off)

```bash
agent-skills project list                 # every skill: its stacks, whether it fits, installed or disabled
agent-skills project disable wcag-audit   # removed for every agent; init leaves it out from then on
agent-skills project enable load-test     # installed even when the stack does not call for it
```

Both switches take `--dry-run` and are kept in `.skribly/agent-skills.json`, so the next `init` respects them. A skill without stacks fits every project; the stacks of each skill are on its page under [All skills](/skills/skill/).

## 5. Keep the lessons

[Section titled “5. Keep the lessons”](#5-keep-the-lessons)

A lesson is one line in `.skribly/lessons.md` under a scope heading: `## [All]`, `## [CI]` or `## [<module>]`, where a module is a folder name, a path or a glob. The agent proposes one at the end of `task`, `test-loop`, `review` and `debug`; [`learn`](/skills/skill/learn/) saves it after your OK, with the date and the skill it came from.

```text
Lesson (pitfall, scope src/cart, src/cart/price.ts:41): prices are integers in cents; never parse them as floats. Save? [y/N]
```

Pick the narrowest scope that is still true: every skill then reads only the lessons for the files it changes. Guesses and one-off facts are not lessons, and anything that looks like a secret is refused. Ask `/learn` to list, prune or promote lessons into the profile.

## 6. Add project skills

[Section titled “6. Add project skills”](#6-add-project-skills)

When the project has a ritual of its own (a release step, a data refresh, a module scaffold), `train-skills` proposes a small skill for it:

* named `<project>-<topic>` in lowercase, never the name of a library skill;
* one `SKILL.md` in `.agents/skills/<name>/`, with a `name`, a `description` that says when to use it, and at most 40 lines of steps, each citing the file or command it comes from;
* shown to you before it is written, and written only after your OK. Claude Code reads `.claude/skills/`, so the agent asks whether it should go there too.

Later sessions refine it with `learn`. Nothing is installed or published from it: it stays in the repository, for the people who work in it.

## Read next

[Section titled “Read next”](#read-next)

* [How it works](/skills/how-it-works/): the pipeline, the guardrails, the profile and the lessons.
* [Updates](/skills/updates/): keep the skills current.
* [Troubleshooting](/skills/troubleshooting/): `agent-skills doctor` names each problem with its fix.

# Troubleshooting agent-skills

> Fixes for common agent-skills problems - agents that do not see skills, install conflicts, Windows links, tracker errors, the commit hook and optional tools.

## The agent does not see the skills

[Section titled “The agent does not see the skills”](#the-agent-does-not-see-the-skills)

* Run `agent-skills doctor`: it shows which agents were detected and where skills are installed.
* Restart the agent or start a new chat; most agents scan skill folders at startup.
* Check the location for your agent in [Supported agents](/skills/agents/). Older versions may need `--format rules`.
* Codex lists a skill twice: old copies sit in the deprecated `~/.codex/skills`. `doctor` warns about them; remove them.
* Cursor, OpenCode or Copilot list a skill twice in a project: they also read `.claude/skills`. Install Claude at user scope and the others at project scope, or the reverse.

## `agent-skills: command not found`

[Section titled “agent-skills: command not found”](#agent-skills-command-not-found)

Run `npm link` in the repository, call `node ~/agent-skills/cli/agent-skills.mjs`, or link `bin/agent-skills` into a folder on `PATH` (`ln -s ~/agent-skills/bin/agent-skills ~/.local/bin/`). On Windows use `bin\agent-skills.cmd`.

## “exists and was not installed by agent-skills”

[Section titled ““exists and was not installed by agent-skills””](#exists-and-was-not-installed-by-agent-skills)

A file or folder with the same name was already there, so it was left alone. Compare it, then rerun with `--force`; the old one is moved to `<path>.bak-agent-skills`.

## `sync` or `uninstall` skips a copy I edited

[Section titled “sync or uninstall skips a copy I edited”](#sync-or-uninstall-skips-a-copy-i-edited)

On purpose: hand-edited copies are never overwritten or deleted. Keep your edit, or use `--force` to replace or remove it.

## Links on Windows

[Section titled “Links on Windows”](#links-on-windows)

User-scope installs create folder junctions, which need no administrator rights or developer mode. If a junction cannot be created, for example on some network drives, install with `--copy` and run `agent-skills sync` after updates.

## WSL and Windows at the same time

[Section titled “WSL and Windows at the same time”](#wsl-and-windows-at-the-same-time)

Each environment has its own home folder and agents. Install in both, from one clone if you like, running `agent-skills install` inside each environment.

## Tracker problems

[Section titled “Tracker problems”](#tracker-problems)

* `access denied (HTTP 401/403)`: a wrong or expired token, or a missing scope. `agent-skills tasks check` tests every tracker.
* `cannot resolve` or `no connection`: VPN or URL. `TLS problem`: set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` to your company’s CA certificate.
* `ENG-12 could be Jira or Linear` (or Skribly Tracker): add `Tracker: jira` (or `linear`, `skribly`) to `.tasks/workflow.md`, set `AGENT_SKILLS_TRACKER`, or pass `--tracker`.
* GitHub without a token: public issues work at 60 requests an hour; private ones need `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `gh auth login`.

## PageSpeed Insights says HTTP 429

[Section titled “PageSpeed Insights says HTTP 429”](#pagespeed-insights-says-http-429)

The keyless quota is shared and often used up. Create an API key for the PageSpeed Insights API and set `PSI_API_KEY`, or measure locally with `--local`, which needs Chrome.

## Playwright or axe-core is missing

[Section titled “Playwright or axe-core is missing”](#playwright-or-axe-core-is-missing)

`browser-check`, `wcag-audit` and `e2e-tests` look for Playwright in the project, then globally. Install it only if you want it: `npm i -D playwright axe-core && npx playwright install chromium`. Without it the skills fall back to manual checklists and say so.

## The commit-msg hook did not run

[Section titled “The commit-msg hook did not run”](#the-commit-msg-hook-did-not-run)

* Run `agent-skills hooks status` in that repository. Hooks are per repository.
* husky, lefthook and similar tools set `core.hooksPath`; add the printed line to their `commit-msg` hook.
* `node` must be on `PATH` for git. GUI clients sometimes have a minimal `PATH`.

## Does it send my code anywhere?

[Section titled “Does it send my code anywhere?”](#does-it-send-my-code-anywhere)

No. The CLI talks only to your tracker (when you fetch, or explicitly post), to OSV.dev or PageSpeed Insights when you run those audits, and to package registries through your own package manager. Nothing else is collected or uploaded.

## How do I use it in a team?

[Section titled “How do I use it in a team?”](#how-do-i-use-it-in-a-team)

Install at project scope (`--project .`) and commit `.claude/skills` and `.agents/skills`, so everyone gets the same skills. `.tasks/` stays personal. Put shared conventions (base branch, commit pattern, check commands) in `AGENTS.md`, and each developer’s `.tasks/workflow.md` is proposed from them. Each developer installs the commit hook in their own clone.

# Updates

> How to keep agent-skills current - git pull and sync today, and the planned agent-skills update command and plugin marketplaces of Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI.

agent-skills is a git repository. Updating it means getting the newer files and letting the CLI apply them to every place it installed skills.

## Update today

[Section titled “Update today”](#update-today)

```bash
cd ~/agent-skills && git pull && agent-skills sync     # every recorded install, user and project scope
agent-skills sync --dry-run                            # what sync would change, without changing it
agent-skills doctor                                    # what is installed where, each problem with its fix
```

* **User scope** installs are symlinks to the repository, so `git pull` alone updates the skills you have; `sync` re-applies each recorded install.
* **Project scope** installs are copies, so they change only when `sync` runs. A file you edited by hand is kept unless you pass `--force`; with `--force` it is first moved to `<path>.bak-agent-skills`.
* `sync` re-applies the skills each install already has. A new skill comes with `agent-skills install --skills <name>`, or in a project with `agent-skills init` run again, which adds the skills that fit the stack and keeps your `project disable` and `project enable` choices.

Every install is recorded in `~/.config/agent-skills/installs.json`, so `sync` knows every place to refresh. Restart the agent (or open a new chat) afterwards so it reads its skills folder again.

## Planned: `agent-skills update`

[Section titled “Planned: agent-skills update”](#planned-agent-skills-update)

Planned

The commands in this section are planned for the next release and do not exist yet.

* **Install without cloning by hand**: `npx github:skribly/agent-skills install --target all`, with no npm package needed.
* **`agent-skills update`**: fetches the newest release tag of the repository and runs `sync`, in one command.
* **Releases on a tag**: each version is published on GitHub from its tag, with its changelog.

## Planned: plugin marketplaces

[Section titled “Planned: plugin marketplaces”](#planned-plugin-marketplaces)

The same `skills/` folder will also be described for the agents that install and update skills packs themselves:

| Agent       | Planned manifest                                | What it gives you                                      |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Claude Code | a plugin and a marketplace (`.claude-plugin/`)  | add the marketplace once; Claude Code updates the pack |
| Codex CLI   | a plugin manifest (`.codex-plugin/`)            | Codex installs and updates the pack                    |
| Gemini CLI  | an extension manifest (`gemini-extension.json`) | Gemini CLI installs and updates the extension          |

Until then, `git pull && agent-skills sync` covers every agent.

## Read next

[Section titled “Read next”](#read-next)

* [Install](/skills/install/): user scope or project scope, Windows, removing everything.
* [Train the skills for your project](/skills/train/): `init` and the project switches.
* [Changelog](/changelog/): what changed in each release.

# Skribly Tracker

> The issue tracker of the Skribly ecosystem - workspaces, projects, issues, workflows, roles, boards, comments and time logs, with a REST API designed for coding agents.

**Skribly Tracker** plans the work that the rest of Skribly carries out: projects, issues with keys like `AGENT-12`, Kanban boards, comments and time logs. It runs in the browser, and its REST API is designed for coding agents as much as for people.

![The Kanban board of a sample project with four columns: To do, In progress, Review and Done](/_astro/tracker-board.ByjEJGOM_Z1Ji1yG.webp)

Status

First release, 0.1. The browser interface, the REST API v1 with personal access tokens, signed webhooks, the Docker stack and the agent-skills `skribly` tracker work today. The released version runs on PHP 8.4 and Laravel 12 with MySQL 8.4; moving it to the shared Node.js stack is planned and would keep the same API.

## Concepts

[Section titled “Concepts”](#concepts)

| Concept             | What it is                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Workspace**       | The top level that holds projects and people                                                                                                                                           |
| **Project**         | A set of issues with a short key such as `AGENT` or `WEB`, its own workflow, labels and members                                                                                        |
| **Issue**           | A unit of work with a key made of the project key and a number, like `AGENT-12`. It has a type, status, priority, labels, assignee, reporter, estimate, due date, parent and subtasks. |
| **Issue type**      | `task`, `bug` or `feature`                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Priority**        | `lowest`, `low`, `medium`, `high` or `urgent`                                                                                                                                          |
| **Status**          | A column of the project’s workflow. *To do, In progress, Review, Done* by default.                                                                                                     |
| **Status category** | Each status belongs to `todo`, `in_progress` or `done`. “Open” means not done.                                                                                                         |
| **Comment**         | Markdown text on an issue                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Time entry**      | Hours logged on an issue with a date, a comment and an activity: `development`, `review`, `testing`, `design`, `meeting` or `other`                                                    |
| **Watcher**         | A person who follows an issue without being assigned                                                                                                                                   |
| **Attachment**      | A file on an issue, up to 10 MB by default                                                                                                                                             |
| **Activity log**    | Every change to an issue, with who made it and when                                                                                                                                    |

## Workflow

[Section titled “Workflow”](#workflow)

Each project has its own workflow in **Project → Settings → Workflow**. Admins can rename, reorder and add statuses, and give each one a category. Any status of the issue’s project can be set; there are no fixed transitions.

## Roles

[Section titled “Roles”](#roles)

| Role       | What it can do                                                            |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Admin**  | Everything, plus projects, workflows, people and webhooks                 |
| **Member** | Create and work on issues: edit, comment, assign, change status, log time |
| **Viewer** | Read only                                                                 |

API tokens act with their owner’s role, and can be made read-only on top of it. See [Personal access tokens](/tracker/tokens/).

## Views

[Section titled “Views”](#views)

| View          | What it shows                                                                                                                                |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Dashboard** | Your open issues, watched issues, projects and recent activity                                                                               |
| **Board**     | A Kanban board with drag and drop between the columns of the project’s workflow. With a keyboard, open an issue and change its status there. |
| **List**      | Filters, search and sorting, shared with the API                                                                                             |
| **Issue**     | Markdown description, subtasks, comments, time log, attachments and history                                                                  |
| **Profile**   | Language, theme and API tokens                                                                                                               |

The interface is in Polish and English, with light and dark themes that follow the system and switch from the top bar, and an accessibility panel on every page for text size, contrast, fonts and motion. WCAG 2.2 AA is the target.

## Connect the other tools

[Section titled “Connect the other tools”](#connect-the-other-tools)

### Skribly Agent

[Section titled “Skribly Agent”](#skribly-agent)

Skribly Tracker is the default tracker of Skribly Agent. Add a Skribly Tracker account with the address and a read-write token. Tasks assigned to you appear in the app, which can comment, change status, assign and log time. See [Personal access tokens](/tracker/tokens/).

### agent-skills

[Section titled “agent-skills”](#agent-skills)

The `task` skill reads this tracker like any other. Put the address and token in `~/.config/agent-skills/credentials.env`:

```bash
SKRIBLY_TRACKER_URL=http://localhost:8100
SKRIBLY_TRACKER_TOKEN=...
```

Then run `agent-skills tasks check`, and `/task AGENT-12` in your agent. See [Trackers](/skills/trackers/#skribly-tracker).

## Built for agents

[Section titled “Built for agents”](#built-for-agents)

* The REST API maps one call to one method of Skribly Agent’s tracker client, and to the agent-skills `task` skill. See the [mapping](/tracker/rest-api/#skribly-agent-mapping).
* Issue keys are case-insensitive and a leading `#` is ignored, so an agent can paste what it reads.
* Descriptions and comments are Markdown, returned exactly as written.
* `updated_since` lets a client poll for changes cheaply.
* Signed [webhooks](/tracker/webhooks/) tell any service when issues change.
